C-2F826067-BFCA-4D10-9B62-497E7E5A6EEE.html:
There was a "KITEC" sticker in the electrical panel. This indicates that the home was or may have been originally piped with KITEC pipe and fittings. These fittings were the subject of a class action lawsuit where a fund was established to have homes with KITEC to be re-piped.  Some homes were re-piped, some homes were not.  When we encounter homes with this sticker we look for signs of a re-pipe.  This home appears to have been re-piped as evidenced by the new pipes in the attic.

For more information on KITEC fittings and the lawsuit go to : http://www.plumbingdefect.com/

C-51C30E39-DE22-4944-B7C6-9A1E274B8EB0.name: What Is a Condensation Drain Line
C-51C30E39-DE22-4944-B7C6-9A1E274B8EB0.html:
A condensate drain line helps remove excess water that drips off of your air conditioner's evaporator unit.

When your air conditioner removes humid air from the living space through your return vents to be cooled, water droplets form on the evaporator coils (the part that's cooling the air).


This water is collected into a condensation drain pan which funnels the water into a PVC drain line to be carried out of the home. If the drain pan or drain line becomes clogged or obstructed it can allow water to fill in the pan and overflow, dripping onto the attic ceiling and causing damage and moisture problems.

C-571A3CC0-FA25-4F08-B15F-85BB949296D3.html: Aluminum wire is installed on 120 VAC branch electrical circuits in the subject house. These single strand, branch circuit aluminum wires were used widely in houses during the mid 1960s and 1970s. According to the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, problems due to expansion can cause overheating at connections between the wire and devices (switches and outlets) or at splices, which has resulted in fires. For further information on aluminum wiring contact the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission via the Internet at http://www.cpsc.gov/ . It is recommended that the electrical system be evaluated by a licensed electrical contractor.

C-5EC924FB-69AD-49D3-BFE2-55124564F944.html:
There was efflorescence and concrete that was beginning to deteriorate on the perimeter wall. 

Efflorescence is the migration of a salt to the surface of a porous material, where it forms a coating. This typically occurs in cinder block or stucco walls when moisture from a constant source such as irrigation allows water to evaporate, trapping the minerals behind in the wall.

C-5F53B6D7-6525-4BB1-AA10-48382FF2509B.name: Running Toilet
C-5F53B6D7-6525-4BB1-AA10-48382FF2509B.html: The toilet was constantly running due to a poor seal in the tank at the flapper. As the tank water level slowly dropped, the auto fill feature kicked in to refill it. Causing the tank's water level to constantly lower and rise. This can cause a large increase to the water bill as gallons of water can be wasted over the course of an entire water bill cycle. We recommend repairing or replacing the tank flapper or other parts as needed to ensure the tank is water tight and functions as designed.

C-6B46281E-C54D-43CC-A3FE-5B6478037B0D.name: Pool disclaimer
C-6B46281E-C54D-43CC-A3FE-5B6478037B0D.html:
Pools are fun, but children and adults can lose their life quickly. Over 4000 lives annually are lost with one-third under the age of 14. A child can drown in the time it takes to answer a phone. A swimming pool is 14 times more likely than a motor vehicle to be involved in the death of a child age 4 and under. An estimated 5,000 children ages 14 and under are hospitalized due to near-drownings each year; 15 percent die in the hospital and as many as 20 percent suffer severe, permanent brain damage. Of all preschoolers who drown, 70 percent are in the care of one or both parents at the time of the drowning and 75 percent are missing from sight for five minutes or less. Drowning surpasses all other causes of death to children age 14 and under in Arizona, California, Florida, Hawaii, Montana, Nevada, Oregon, Utah and Washington.

A pool alarm with a loud speaker system to sound outside as well as inside the home could save a life. Even if you do not have children you should be concerned. 35% of children that drowned did so in someone else's pool. For more info, do an Internet search on pool safety or visit this website: http://www.ihf.org/foryourhealth/article_children.html

C-77E23306-DE79-4E06-801E-6450F5B33DEB.name: Electrical SOP
C-77E23306-DE79-4E06-801E-6450F5B33DEB.html: The home inspector shall observe: Service entrance conductors; Service equipment, grounding equipment, main over current device, and main and distribution panels; Amperage and voltage ratings of the service; Branch circuit conductors, their over current devices, and the compatibility of their ampacities and voltages; The operation of a representative number of installed ceiling fans, lighting fixtures, switches and receptacles located inside the house, garage, and on the dwelling's exterior walls; The polarity and grounding of all receptacles within six feet of interior plumbing fixtures, and all receptacles in the garage or carport, and on the exterior of inspected structures; The operation of ground fault circuit interrupters; and Smoke detectors. The home inspector shall describe: Service amperage and voltage; Service entry conductor materials; Service type as being overhead or underground; and Location of main and distribution panels. The home inspector shall report any observed aluminum branch circuit wiring. C-866401A6-65E4-47B9-A786-0FE564853F63.name: Polybutylene
C-866401A6-65E4-47B9-A786-0FE564853F63.html:
The home appears to have been plumbed with Polybutylene Plumbing. There were no signs or indications of any leak or failure in this system.

No matter what type of plumbing material is used in a home (Copper, galvanized steel, PVC, various types of plastic tubing, etc.) they can and have all had failures.  Polybutylene is a type of plastic tubing that was used in the late 70's and into the 90's and is in millions of homes, most of which have had no issues. PB, as is true with other products, can fail and has had failures. The Polybutylene plastic plumbing supply lines (PB 2110) that were installed in this house have the trade name Vanguard).

As with other plumbing products, (and other building products in general)  there was class action litigation brought against the manufacturer.  Some number of homeowners encountered minor to severe leaks, leading to lawsuit(s), which is now closed.

We saw no signs of a problem but do recommend a further evaluation by a licensed plumber who could give you a more qualified opinion of the system.

You may also contact Plumbing Claims Group -- 800-356-3496 or click on the following link for detailed information, background and history on PB 2110 plumbing.     http://www.nachi.org/forum/f22/help-polybutylene-pipes-6938/

As with other plumbing products, (and other building products in general)  there was class action litigation brought against the manufacturer.  Some number of homeowners encountered minor to severe leaks, leading to lawsuit(s), which is now closed.
We saw no signs of a problem but do recommend a further evaluation by a licensed plumber who could give you a more qualified opinion of the system.
You may also contact Plumbing Claims Group -- 800-356-3496 or click on the following link for detailed information, background and history on PB 2110 plumbing.     http://www.nachi.org/forum/f22/help-polybutylene-pipes-6938/

C-9CDCC8CB-33F0-4834-A29A-09FC9D6F2211.name: Improper Sediment Trap
C-9CDCC8CB-33F0-4834-A29A-09FC9D6F2211.html:
The sediment trap on the gas line was installed in the wrong orientation. We recommend this be installed to prevent debris from passing through the line into the unit.

Sediment traps are designed to cause the gas flow to change direction 90 degree at the sediment collection point, thus causing the solid or liquid contaminants to drop out of the gas flow. The nipple and cap should not be placed in the branch opening of a tee fitting because this would not create a change in direction of flow and would allow debris to simply pass/jump over the capped nipple collection point. Example photos are attached.

C-A584E4B8-0FE5-43B0-BA1E-9467BF158F1F.name: evolution of older house GFCI
C-A584E4B8-0FE5-43B0-BA1E-9467BF158F1F.html:
A representative number of outlets within six feet of interior plumbing fixtures or in the garage or on the exterior of the structure were tested and were wired correctly with proper polarity and grounding.  This was the rule before the advent of the GFCI.  The majority of your outlets are grounded, but not all.

Some, most, receptacles were wired without a ground, at the time of construction, which was in 1959, before grounded plugs were used,  (two prong receptacles).  Within six feet of plumbing, these receptacles were equipped with a ground wire on the box within the wall.  Later, some of the outlets (all but a handful) were supplied with a ground.  All outlets have been later supplied with the modern three prong plug, but a few remain ungrounded.

C-F3610757-B240-4F05-9AB2-76132D8A45B4.name: Bonding Wire: Bad
C-F3610757-B240-4F05-9AB2-76132D8A45B4.html: The pool motor's bonding wires were missing or not mounted to the motor casing as designed. We recommend having a bonding wire attached. Bonding is defined as: ”The practice of intentionally electrically connecting all exposed metallic items not designed to carry electricity in a room or building as protection from electric shock.”. Another way of putting it is that the primary purpose of bonding is to keep people and electricity separated. Stray currents (or electrical gradients) can occur in a swimming pool. Every metal component, the pool water and your body are all conductive and will carry electricity in the right situation. In an improperly bonded pool stray currents are out of control and will seek the easiest path for conductivity. A bonded pool balances the electrical pressure and keeps all currents flowing outward into a bonding wire or grid where they are safely dispersed.

II-0081433A-9331-447B-B836-844BBA510981.title: GARAGE WALLS (INCLUDING FIREWALL SEPARATION)
II-0081433A-9331-447B-B836-844BBA510981.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Check for firewall separation when the garage wall is integral with the home's wall or another unit/condo.

2. Do you have a clear view to inspect all areas in the Garage?

3. Check the garage wall for vehicle damage or material knocked loose at the soleplate.

4. Look for bowed paneling which would be typical of a room with higher moisture levels than the rest of home.

More Info:

  1. Black flash marks on or around an outlet on the wall should be noted.
  2. Understand the difficulties of removing old wall paper.
  3. Note areas where there are bedded nails, and seams where they were not sanded down smooth before painting.
  4. Understand that some walls have oil based paint on them andall buyers are planning to use latex which means their paint job will fail.
  5. Oil can go over oil based or latex. Latex cannot go over oil based paint.
  6. There is a product that is a sealer/primer that would need to go over oil based paint and then latex can be applied.

Reference Materials:

II-00EC895E-E582-44DD-8335-DA458F4BAFA8.title: DECKS, BALCONIES, STOOPS, STEPS, AREAWAYS,  PORCHES AND APPLICABLE RAILINGS
II-00EC895E-E582-44DD-8335-DA458F4BAFA8.helpHtml: Inspect slowly paying attention to ceiling, walls, floors and supports. Inspect column(s) 360 degrees for deterioration. Move away any bush that may be hiding trapped moisture. Newly painted areas on wood should be checked with finger pressure at suspicious areas. Check to see if rails are secure.

II-01CE4AF5-611B-4E98-9CB7-B5818F95F822.title: ROOF STRUCTURE AND ATTIC
II-01CE4AF5-611B-4E98-9CB7-B5818F95F822.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Note any stains around chimney or vent pipes in attic. Is there mold or moisture present?

2. Is there any loose wiring in the attic?

3. Is there any knob and tube wiring in the attic? They should not be covered with insulation.

4. Are the bath and range exhaust fans venting to the outside air?

5. Is there a whole house fan or a thermostatically controlled fan in attic?

6. Is there an air handler in attic? Filter? Drip pan? Float switch obstructed in drip pan?

7. Is insulation installed right side up? (Paper side faces the heated space)

8. Are pull-down stairs to the attic mounted properly to ceiling joists at hinge points? Are nuts tight at each step?

9. Does attic access fit the opening or seal opening properly?

10. Note the absence (or condition) of firewall separation in attic when building is multi-family.

11. Are plywood clips missing between sheets of plywood (if sags are apparent)?

12. Is there any loose wiring or exposed splices at the whole house fan?

13. Note any catch pans or containers in the attic that may indicate periodic leaks

14. Note if rafters are 2 x 4 but not truss construction. Usually found in some older homes and can allow sagging of roof.

More Info:

  • Take your time and trace out the rafters with your light. Move around in all areas accessible. The area you don't check, is the area you missed. Don't miss anything. It pays to have a good flashlight and a back up.
  • Always note fire damage in the attic. And do a stab test to determine the strength. Sometimes the "Char" is only skin deep and it looks worse than it is. If you think it's strong, say so. If not, then recommend an engineer and repairs.
  • Sags can occur where:
    • a plywood clip is missing,
    • a truss is damaged,
    • rafters are spaced too far apart,
    • there is a bad crown in the wood or
    • you have a weak piece of plywood.
  • Undersized wood such as a "2 x 4 rafter" spanned too far can create sag. A knee wall or reinforcement would be suggested.
  • This is also a good time to spot wet signs on insulation to alert you of a possible leak. Also scan for wiring splices and exhaust fan ventilation as well as clearance of insulation around recessed "can" lights.
  • The chimney area often shows stains on wood from previously failed flashing orfrom current. indirect light seen at flashing is sometimes not where it is leaking.
  • Ridge line can show leaks where blow-in occurred or from faulty seams or from end caps being missing.
  • This is a good time to trace out the ceiling exhaust fan vent pipes where possible.

Reference Materials:

II-02ACA08E-87D9-4111-A1F4-0D6BFF1F176C.title: WALLS (Structural)
II-02ACA08E-87D9-4111-A1F4-0D6BFF1F176C.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1.(Older home), Push on the wood covered with plaster, or wood with other coverings, on a wall near a window, to see if it has "give" to it and to see if you suspect deterioration or termite damage.

2. Bowed paneling on a wall alerts you to moisture or possible water intrusion.

3. Faint water signs can sometimes be found under windows and along baseboards.

More Information:

Walls can tell you a lot about the house. Settlement cracks in plaster or coverings should be noted as minor or significant in relation to the structure or to the wall covering as whether or not a repair is needed.

Reference Materials:

II-04863B83-9CEF-4D07-8A18-9B53CDAFD4D9.title: NORMAL OPERATING CONTROLS
II-04863B83-9CEF-4D07-8A18-9B53CDAFD4D9.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

Check the thermostat for damage or operation. See if the kill switch on air handler works.

More Info:

II-05162680-5B1C-4256-B077-FFD176B10B78.title: FOUNDATIONS, BASEMENTS AND CRAWLSPACES (Report signs of abnormal or harmful water penetration into the building or signs of abnormal or harmful condensation on building components.)
II-05162680-5B1C-4256-B077-FFD176B10B78.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Check brick and mortar of the foundation at all downspout locations.

2. Notice any new downspouts or splashblocks that may alert you to check for previous water intrusion once inside the basement or crawlspace.

3. Is there a vapor barrier (6 mil recommended) on the dirt floor of the basement or crawlspace?

4. Note water stains on the inside wall of the crawlspace or basement as to whether or not they indicate current intrusion.

5. Are there standing water stains on the plastic?

6. Mold or Fungi on joists indicates a moisture problem and moisture should be noted in your report. Whether or not you use the word mold, fungi, wood destroying organisms or mildew is up to you. The word mildew is used to describe the type of fungi that can only grow on fruit. Mildew should not be used in a inspection report.

7. Note the absence (or condition) of the firewall separation in a crawlspace or basement, when the building is a multi-family dwelling.

8. Look for an undercut foundation where someone might have dug below the original footing to create a basement. Sometimes they stucco the dirt wall with cement which is brittle and is not adequate. Also look for support piers where dirt was dug away around the footing.

9. Look for water stains on table legs, shelving and the bottom of the stair stringer for indications of water intrusion.

More Info:

Foundation cracks: Hair-line cracks are generally okay as long as there aren't many or if they are old. Usually, all settlement cracks occur within the first three years after a home is built. Most of the time you are looking at an old crack. To help eliminate concerns about a crack ask yourself:

  1. Are there any water intrusion signs?
  2. Are there cracks on the other remaining walls?
  3. If a wall is painted, is there paint in the crack as old as the paint on the wall? No paint in crack could mean a fresh crack.


Astair-step crack is usually the least significant. Avertical crack is a little more concerning but not as bad as ahorizontal crack.A horizontal crack with a dirt bank on the other side of the wall is the worse type of crack. You can take a straight edge (sometimes the seller has a board in his basement) and hold it vertical against the cracked wall. There will be a gap between the straight edge and the block that gives you an idea of how much the wall has moved because of the load behind it. A 1/4 inch gap or bigger in the crack raises a concern as well. On the other hand, there are plenty of homes with hairline cracks and they are generally fine. You need to consider when to ask for a structural engineer and when to say they are typical settlement cracks. Moisture on a wall can also increase the likelihood of further settlement. This opinion is based on my experience living in the Southeast US. When in doubt, recommend an engineer. It would be cheaper for you to be embarrassed and pay $300 for an engineer's wasted trip (worse case scenario), than to be wrong about the severity of settlement and be sued for thousands.

Always check the basement or crawlspace last (after you run water from all fixtures inside) to find leaks. When you do enter the crawlspace:

  1. look at each inside wall to the left and right of the entryway for water or mud marks on wall.
  2. If the basement entry is below grade with steps, check to see if a floor drain exists and does it appear to work properly.
  3. Water intrusion signs are found along the foundation wall as a water line or stain.
  4. Silt travel on plastic or ground should be mentioned.
  5. Sometimes stains are seen under a foundation vent on wall.
  6. Water intrusion throws up a red alert to as to whether or not mold is growing.
  7. Sump pumps don't always remove all the water. Or all the water doesn't always travel to the sump pump.
  8. In the basement, look for water stains on walls or wooden legs of a shelf or work table.
  9. Sometimes water seeps in through the wall or pin holes.
  10. Old brick foundation walls have a hard time keeping the water out.

As a general rule, you should try your best to include a comment about water intrusion or signs. Each inspection, see if you can discover any type of silt or dirt stains on block wall or support piers. Include new construction where you are confident that the stains are likely from before the roof was installed and rain water fell into the inside of foundation walls. All stains should be mentioned in the report.

Reference Materials:

The Home Inspector shall observe structural components including foundations, floors, walls, columns or piers, ceilings and roof. The home inspector shall describe the type of Foundation, floor structure, wall structure, columns or piers, ceiling structure, roof structure. The home inspector shall: Probe structural components where deterioration is suspected; Enter under floor crawl spaces, basements, and attic spaces except when access is obstructed, when entry could damage the property, or when dangerous or adverse situations are suspected; Report the methods used to observe under floor crawl spaces and attics; and Report signs of abnormal or harmful water penetration into the building or signs of abnormal or harmful condensation on building components.

The home inspector is not required to: Enter any area or perform any procedure that may damage the property or its components or be dangerous to or adversely effect the health of the home inspector or other persons.

II-053664CD-F351-415E-9976-472B27A50CBB.title: WALLS
II-053664CD-F351-415E-9976-472B27A50CBB.helpHtml: The home inspector shall observe: Walls, ceiling, and floors; Steps, stairways, balconies, and railings; Counters and a representative number of cabinets; and A representative number of doors and windows. The home inspector shall: Operate a representative number of windows and interior doors; and Report signs of abnormal or harmful water penetration into the building or signs of abnormal or harmful condensation on building components. The home inspector is not required to observe: Paint, wallpaper, and other finish treatments on the interior walls, ceilings, and floors;  Carpeting; or Draperies, blinds, or other window treatments.

II-05FAB5DD-E4F2-4B6D-8CDF-835FD3596DE0.title: PRESENCE OF INSTALLED COOLING SOURCE IN EACH ROOM
II-05FAB5DD-E4F2-4B6D-8CDF-835FD3596DE0.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

More Info:

  1. Don't miss the absence of a vent in a room or you could be sued and be liable for the cost to put one in.
  2. One must also consider: Why isn't one there? It could be the size of the heat/AC unit which would require a bigger unit or perhaps there is no physical way to install one. Extreme remodeling may be involved.
  3. Also, stay alert for the type of heating system in the house with an AC condenser. If it's boiler heat and there is an AC unit outside, and the house is 2 story, it is likely that the AC serves the upstairs only. Therefore it is necessary to point this out in your report.

Reference Materials:

II-07DAB40A-87C5-4DB7-9646-6BFF92B62D35.title: GARAGE DOOR (S)
II-07DAB40A-87C5-4DB7-9646-6BFF92B62D35.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is there any staining or discoloration that warrants a finger pressure test on exterior door trim /jambs at bottom ?

2. Does the garage door opening height and width seem normal?

3. The garage door must reverse when met with resistance regardless of whether or not they have sensors. Sensors should be no higher off the floor than 6" or according to manufacturer specs.

4. What is the condition of the weather-stripping at garage door floor and sides?

5. Check both sides of Garage door for damage?

6. The "jerk and let go" test for the garage door works best but there is a risk of damaging the door if you don't let go quick enough. A 2 x 4 block placed on floor can damage a metal door if door does not reverse (not recommended).

8. Note older garage door springs that do not have retention cables to contain the spring if the cable breaks.

More Info:

  1. Always open and shut a door from both sides and note whether or not the door latches.
  2. Also note if the door is out of square enough that it no longer ensures privacy.
  3. Check for holes in doors and for a doorstop on each one. Note any trim or hardware missing (check all doors).
  4. Basement or Crawlspace: Make sure that the door fits properly and is properly painted. Look at the ground in front of the door for negative slope that may allow water intrusion.
  5. Check to see if the door is delaminating or deteriorated at the bottom .
  6. Sliding glass and patio doors: Open and close doors as needed and check for "daylight" and continuous weather-stripping.
  7. Also, close the door with knob until it latches. Then turn deadbolt and check strike for proper alignment and a tight fit.
  8. Also look carefully at the glass, and check for "Cloudy" appearance or cracked glass. This is a good time to inspect the floor area around door for possible water intrusion or deterioration.
  9. Garage doors: Raise the garage door and lay a 2 x 4 block on the floor at the middle of the door opening (except a metal door that could be damaged by a 2 x 4 block). Document if the door reverses or not.
  10. If you use your hand to provide resistance and the door does not reverse, you can severely damage the door if you're not careful. The door can "fold-up" damaging the door panel and chain drive.
  11. Even if the door has electronic sensors, it still should reverse when met with resistance. Adjustment screws are usually found on the side and rear of opener. These door adjustment screws can be tricky to adjust.

Reference Materials:

II-0A03EBB9-1F5A-4E0C-8858-92254894B959.helpHtml:

1. Note if door does not afford protection such as a fire rated door.

II-0BACE309-62E0-42DB-8BA7-E3231E803B5A.title: POLARITY AND GROUNDING OF RECEPTACLES WITHIN 6 FEET OF INTERIOR PLUMBING FIXTURES, AND ALL RECEPTACLES IN GARAGE, CARPORT,  EXTERIOR WALLS OF INSPECTED STRUCTURE
II-0BACE309-62E0-42DB-8BA7-E3231E803B5A.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Do you notice any GFCI outlets with freezers plugged into them? Don't forget to reset GFCI. Two prong plugs in the Garage or around any areas with water?

More Info:

  1. I use a simple three-prong plug with a GFCI test button. It identifies whether or not the outlet is grounded, and if the polarity is correct.
  2. Some tips are: Your three-prong GFCI test plug will not "trip" the outlet if it is a non-grounded GFCI. But it still should trip by pressing the test button on outlet, and kill the circuit.
  3. A non-grounded outlet can be corrected by either attaching a ground wire to the outlet and attach it to a metal rod or a metal plumbing pipe.
  4. Or, replace the three-prongnon-grounded outlet with a three-prong GFCI outlet. A sticker should be on the outlet that identifies it as non-grounded.
  5. Or last, change the circuit breaker to a GFCI breaker at the panel.
  6. You can "trip" a non-grounded GFCI with a voltmeter by placing one prong of the voltmeter in the short slit of the outlet, and take the other prong of the voltmeter and touch a metal plumbing pipe (that eventually contacts the soil).
  7. Most three-prong GFCI plugs will show two lights at the end of the plug when the outlet being tested is grounded. When you press the button on the plug, both lights should remain lit and strong. If however, the plug lights up only one of the two grounding lights "Faint or Dim" and you press the button on the plug and it shows "Reverse polarity", it may just be a "loose" ground wire and can be corrected a lot easier than having to install a new ground wire.
  8. Just because you can press the test button on the GFCI outlet using your finger and it "trips," doesn't mean it killed the circuit. It could be defective.
  9. New GFCI outlets can be defective when installed.
  10. Always use the three-prong GFCI test plug on every three-prong outlet.
  11. Homeowners frequently use a freezer in their garage. Most outlets in the garage are on a GFCI Circuit. When you're inspecting the home don't forget to reset the GFCI outlet or you may be buying the homeowners spoiled food.

Reference Materials:

II-0BE7E743-AB48-4517-AC10-E1DCDE2D3E01.title: FLOORS (Structural)
II-0BE7E743-AB48-4517-AC10-E1DCDE2D3E01.helpHtml:
Quick Check:


1. Is insulation installed right side up? (Paper side should face the heated space)

2. Did you pull back insulation under the bathroom floors to check for leaks or deterioration?

3. Note any incomplete X bracing of joists

4. (Older homes) Is the main girder supported every 8 feet or at seams?

5. Screw jacks used as permanent support might work, but some inspectors will consider them as "for temporary use only" and will recommend replacement (FYI).

6. Is there construction debris or any discontinued appliances, water heaters or furnaces that need to be noted in the report?

7. Note any floor system repairs that used smaller framing materials than existing joists.

8. Note if joist spacing is 2 feet apart or more which can prevent the installation of insulation or cause a bounce in the floor when walked or when heavy furniture is in the room. You may be inspecting a vacant home and a bounce or sag in the floor could be discovered after the buyer moves in heavy furniture.

More Info:

Inspecting the floor system: Remove insulation and look at these areas to find the jackpot:

1. Where outside faucets are located .
2. Where drain lines are installed from baths and kitchen
3. Where insulation is missing or where newer insulation is installed.
4. Where exterior doors or patio doors are.
5. Where decks attach to outer band of floor system.

Other areas to look for are themain girder (termite damage is found often here). Also where wooden supports might have allowed moisture and termites to crawl up to floor system. Hanging insulation is a sign of moisture condensation if there are several hanging pieces, or a snake. It doesn't hurt to use a stab tool on joists every now and then while you are crawling around. Look on the ground or plastic barrier for evidence of a repair above. Often there are wood crumbs or small debris that was not cleaned up completely.

Reference Materials:

II-0C55DACD-385C-4AB3-80E1-043DCDDDF33F.title: COLUMNS OR PIERS
II-0C55DACD-385C-4AB3-80E1-043DCDDDF33F.helpHtml:
Quick Check:


1.Look for an undercut foundation where someone has dug below the original footing to create a basement. Sometimes they stucco the dirt wall with cement which is brittle and is not adequate. Also look for support piers where dirt was dug away around footing.

2. Screw jacks used as a permanent support might work, but some inspectors will consider them as "for temporary use only" and will recommend replacement (FYI).

3.(Older homes) Is the main girder supported every 8 feet or at seams?

As a general rule there should be a proper support and a proper footing under all girders at each end, and in between about every 6 feet or so. Older homes were spaced about 8 feet. The floor joist should have a proper support at each end. If there are some homemade supports in the middle of some joists, (usually found in older homes), you need to consider why they are there:

  1. Is there something heavy above the floor like a piano or heavy furniture?
  2. Are the floor joists undersized or is the span too far and beginning to sag?
  3. Is there a bounce in the floor above?

Floor joists are not supposed to need any support between the two ends. Theoretically, you should be able to remove those temporary supports. Ask yourself if you would? Or what problem would result? That's how I determine if these temporary supports are really needed. If they are, then they need to have a proper support and footing. Usually a properly installed drop girder that supports several joists at one time is recommended. If I think they are not serving much purpose, I'll note that the temporary supports do not appear to be serving any real support need for the joist.

Reference Materials:

II-0C973BE7-6193-4158-B183-6BD2B5899B87.title: GARAGE WALLS (INCLUDING FIREWALL SEPARATION)
II-0C973BE7-6193-4158-B183-6BD2B5899B87.helpHtml:

2. Do you have a clear view to inspect all areas in the Garage?

3. Check the garage wall for vehicle damage or material knocked loose at the soleplate.

4. Look for bowed paneling which would be typical of a room with higher moisture levels than the rest of home.

More Info:

  1. Black flash marks on or around an outlet on the wall should be noted.
  2. Understand the difficulties of removing old wall paper.
  3. Note areas where there are bedded nails, and seams where they were not sanded down smooth before painting.
  4. Understand that some walls have oil based paint on them andall buyers are planning to use latex which means their paint job will fail.
  5. Oil can go over oil based or latex. Latex cannot go over oil based paint.
  6. There is a product that is a sealer/primer that would need to go over oil based paint and then latex can be applied.

II-0D2570E8-B0B9-411E-A1AA-59F85B18F377.title: SERVICE ENTRANCE AND PANELS
II-0D2570E8-B0B9-411E-A1AA-59F85B18F377.helpHtml: Circuit breaker brand should match the panel brand. An electrical contractor may point this out to your buyer after they purchase the home. I never used to care about mixed brands as long as they fit properly. But clearly on the label, each panel brand requires their own circuit brand only, or it will void the UL listing. This was enough to scare my buyer, and I decided that I would not buy any more breakers. Since then, I've discovered that some electrical contractors feel that some brands can mix because of companies merging. I disagree unless those names are also on that particular panel label. SIEMENS, ITE and GOULD supposedly are one company. MURRAY may also be a part of SIEMENS. WESTINGHOUSE, BRYANT AND CUTLER-HAMMER are supposedly one company. Remember: The electrical panel has a label on it. And somewhere it usually states that only their brand is allowed to be used. All other brands will void warranty or may be a hazard. General Switch Brand panel may allow other brands that will fit. If they do, they will indicate it on the label. When in doubt, recommend an electrical contractor. If a fire was to occur and later found that the source was from the panel and it had different breakers, the homeowner would not be denied the insurance claim. But, the insurance company may feel that the recent inspection should have revealed it. Especially when a UL label on panel states that no other brand is allowed. The insurance company may seek compensation from the inspector in form of litigation. Whether they do or don 't, right is right and wrong is wrong, so I mention it. There should also be a ground wire attached to a driven ground rod at the meter base. This grounds the panel itself. Some local electrical contractors may say that one is really good enough (at plumbing or meter base). But that's true only if the supply lines are not metal (Pex, CPVC etc.). If only the metal plumbing has a ground and not the meter base, and the metal plumbing is old corroded galvanized piping that gets replaced with Pex, there would then be no ground. Or, if the plumber replaced the old piping with copper or metal, it would be up to him to reset the ground and clamp onto the new pipe. And we all know plumbers wouldn't do it.

II-0E474937-DF56-4260-A000-EBC322A048E7.title: DECKS, BALCONIES, STOOPS, STEPS, AREAWAYS,  PORCHES, PATIO/ COVER AND APPLICABLE RAILINGS
II-0E474937-DF56-4260-A000-EBC322A048E7.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is the deck properly bolted to the outer band of the home? Are deck joists supported by a ledger strip or hangers?

2. Check the picket or baluster spacing on the deck and hand/guard rail.

3. Is siding deteriorated where the deck attaches to the home (above deck)?

4. Is there any staining or discoloration that warrants a finger pressure test on soffits, fascia, column bases, window sills, porch flooring or bottom of door jambs?

5. Is there any underpinning of porches or areas that you could not see under?

6. Deck floor covered with outdoor carpet may have underlayment not approved for outdoor use. Decks with awning covers underneath deck to provide a roof may trap water, moisture and cause deterioration that is not accessible to verify.

More Info:

  1. Inspect slowly paying attention to ceiling, walls, floors and supports.
  2. Inspect column(s) 360 degrees for deterioration.
  3. Move away any bush or brush that may be hiding trapped moisture.
  4. Newly painted areas on wood should be checked with finger pressure at suspicious areas.
  5. Check to see if rails are secure. 4 x 4 support posts should not be supporting more than 8 feet high.
  6. Joists should be supported by a ledger or joist hangers.
  7. It is important to see if band of deck is bolted to band of home. If there is siding or wood underlayment in between the deck and house band, the bolts may not be into the meat of the house band enough. Make sure the support posts are notched to receive the band. If not, make sure there is more than nails supporting the band to the post. A general rule to attach deck band to home is to use 5/8" galvanized carriage bolts with washers at each end and every 36 inches or so in between. When you cannot access the inside band of the home to screw the nuts, then 5/8" galvanized lag screws are better than nothing

Reference Materials:

II-109596A6-BCE6-47E4-8D5D-B9F86FF9E1F6.title: CONNECTED DEVICES AND FIXTURES (Observed from a representative number operation of ceiling fans, lighting fixtures, switches and receptacles located inside the house, garage, and on the dwelling's exterior walls)
II-109596A6-BCE6-47E4-8D5D-B9F86FF9E1F6.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is the refrigerator outlet 3 prong plug grounded?

(Baths)
2. Is there a duplex grounded outlet? If not recommend a GFCI when electrical contractor corrects.

3. The light fixture outlet in the bath should be disabled if not grounded.

4. There should be at least two outlets in each room.

5. Note any ceiling fans that wobble more than expected

6. Are there any electric outlets located on the wall above the electric baseboard, which is a possible fire hazard?

More Info:

  1. The inspection item CONNECTED DEVICES AND FIXTURES is for miscellaneous electrical items found around the property. (i.e. loose splices, boxes missing cover plates etc).
  2. I use a simple three-prong plug with a GFCI test button. It identifies whether or not the outlet is grounded, and if the polarity is correct.
  3. Some tips are: Your three-prong GFCI test plug will not "trip" the outlet if it is a non-grounded GFCI. It should still trip by pressing the test button on the outlet, and kill the circuit.
  4. A non-grounded outlet can be corrected by either attaching a ground wire to the outlet and attach it to a metal rod or a metal plumbing pipe.
  5. Or, replace the three-prongnon-grounded outlet with a three-prong GFCI outlet. A sticker should be on the outlet that identifies it as non-grounded.
  6. Or last, change the circuit breaker to a GFCI breaker at panel.
  7. You can "trip" a non-grounded GFCI with a voltmeter by placing one prong of the voltmeter in the short slit of the outlet, and take the other prong of the voltmeter and touch a metal plumbing pipe (that eventually contacts the soil).
  8. Most three-prong GFCI plugs will show two lights at the end of the plug when the outlet being tested is grounded. When you press the button on the plug, both lights should remain lit and strong. If however, the plug lights up only one of the two grounding lights "Faint or Dim" and you press the button on the plug and it shows "Reverse polarity", it may just be a "loose" ground wire and can be corrected a lot easier than having to install a new ground wire.
  9. Just because you can press the test button on the GFCI outlet using your finger and it "trips," doesn't mean it killed the circuit. It could be defective.
  10. New GFCI outlets that are installed can be defective.
  11. Always use the three-prong GFCI test plug on every three-prong outlet.
  12. Homeowners frequently use a freezer in their garage. Most outlets in the garage are on a GFCI Circuit. When you're inspecting the home, don't forget to reset the GFCI outlet or you may be buying the homeowners spoiled food.

II-1263F84C-6BF5-4333-B512-199D139FB275.title: WINDOWS (REPRESENTATIVE NUMBER)
II-1263F84C-6BF5-4333-B512-199D139FB275.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Did you test the windows or write "Not Inspected" when a window has knick-knacks stacked on it?

2. Be sure to note if a window A/C is preventing testing the operation of a window.

3. Are storm windows missing or damaged on single pane windows?

4. Is any weatherstripping missing on windows?

5. Are sash cords missing or replaced with jamb hardware on the windows?

6. Was every accessible window tested for operation? If not, did you note which ones were not tested?

7. Cloudy windows? Note windows that appear cloudy and also note windows that are out of reach and can't be determined if they are cloudy or just dirty.

More Info:

  1. This is where you look for cloudy windows and lock hardware and cracked or loose glass.
  2. Also check the sill for strength against deterioration.
  3. Walls leaking around windows can sometimes be discovered by inspecting the sill for deterioration.

Reference Materials:

II-12877CD8-84FE-4B75-9D4E-54924F6A92DF.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Note if door does not afford protection such as a fire rated door.

More Info:

II-12AC0925-6CFE-4D92-A949-902796D977F9.title: GARAGE CEILINGS
II-12AC0925-6CFE-4D92-A949-902796D977F9.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Be sure to note any ceiling, or projection from a ceiling, in any finished room that is lower than 7 feet from the floor.

More Info:

  1. Look at an old home with an old eye.
  2. Always note water stains
  3. On newer homes, note nail pops, exposed or loose sheetrock tape and repair signs.
  4. Workmanship is important on all homes, but especially new ones.
  5. Look for signs of only one coat of paint, poor sanding, nail indentations etc.
  6. Look at the perimeter of the floor for water stains or deterioration.

Reference Materials:

The home inspector shall observe: Walls, ceiling, and floors; Steps, stairways, balconies, and railings; Counters and a representative number of cabinets; and A representative number of doors and windows. The home inspector shall: Operate a representative number of windows and interior doors; and Report signs of abnormal or harmful water penetration into the building or signs of abnormal or harmful condensation on building components.

The home inspector is not required to observe: Paint, wallpaper, and other finish treatments on the interior walls, ceilings, and floors; Carpeting; or Draperies, blinds, or other window treatments.

II-15BE6444-E5D7-4ED9-A619-5C401FD72081.title: PRESENCE OF INSTALLED COOLING SOURCE IN EACH ROOM
II-15BE6444-E5D7-4ED9-A619-5C401FD72081.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

More Info:

  1. Don't miss the absence of a vent in a room or you could be sued and be liable for the cost to put one in.
  2. One must also consider: Why isn't one there? It could be the size of the heat/AC unit which would require a bigger unit or perhaps there is no physical way to install one. Extreme remodeling may be involved.
  3. Also, stay alert for the type of heating system in the house with an AC condenser. If it's boiler heat and there is an AC unit outside, and the house is 2 story, it is likely that the AC serves the upstairs only. Therefore it is necessary to point this out in your report.

II-1C9DDC67-9168-4479-854E-AFBC153DF5CB.title: GARAGE DOOR (S)
II-1C9DDC67-9168-4479-854E-AFBC153DF5CB.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is there any staining or discoloration that warrants a finger pressure test on exterior door trim /jambs at bottom ?

2. Does the garage door opening height and width seem normal?

3. The garage door must reverse when met with resistance regardless of whether or not they have sensors. Sensors should be no higher off the floor than 6" or according to manufacturer specs.

4. What is the condition of the weather-stripping at garage door floor and sides?

5. Check both sides of Garage door for damage?

6. The "jerk and let go" test for the garage door works best but there is a risk of damaging the door if you don't let go quick enough. A 2 x 4 block placed on floor can damage a metal door if door does not reverse (not recommended).

8. Note older garage door springs that do not have retention cables to contain the spring if the cable breaks.

More Info:

  1. Always open and shut a door from both sides and note whether or not the door latches.
  2. Also note if the door is out of square enough that it no longer ensures privacy.
  3. Check for holes in doors and for a doorstop on each one. Note any trim or hardware missing (check all doors).
  4. Basement or Crawlspace: Make sure that the door fits properly and is properly painted. Look at the ground in front of the door for negative slope that may allow water intrusion.
  5. Check to see if the door is delaminating or deteriorated at the bottom .
  6. Sliding glass and patio doors: Open and close doors as needed and check for "daylight" and continuous weather-stripping.
  7. Also, close the door with knob until it latches. Then turn deadbolt and check strike for proper alignment and a tight fit.
  8. Also look carefully at the glass, and check for "Cloudy" appearance or cracked glass. This is a good time to inspect the floor area around door for possible water intrusion or deterioration.
  9. Garage doors: Raise the garage door and lay a 2 x 4 block on the floor at the middle of the door opening (except a metal door that could be damaged by a 2 x 4 block). Document if the door reverses or not.
  10. If you use your hand to provide resistance and the door does not reverse, you can severely damage the door if you're not careful. The door can "fold-up" damaging the door panel and chain drive.
  11. Even if the door has electronic sensors, it still should reverse when met with resistance. Adjustment screws are usually found on the side and rear of opener. These door adjustment screws can be tricky to adjust.

II-1E6198C4-8359-42ED-A055-1496788B56EE.title: STEPS, STAIRWAYS, BALCONIES AND RAILINGS
II-1E6198C4-8359-42ED-A055-1496788B56EE.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is there a light switch at the top of basement stairs?

2. Stairs to the basement need proper 6'8" of headroom clearance if there is no occupant door in the basement that leads to the outside (general rule).

More Info:

Look for strength of the rails and stairs and proper spacing of balusters (pickets).

Reference Materials:

II-20139FCA-8A7A-4EAA-ACDD-474492E66A9D.title: WALLS (interior and Exterior)
II-20139FCA-8A7A-4EAA-ACDD-474492E66A9D.helpHtml: Walls can tell you a lot about the house. Settlement cracks should be noted as minor or significant in relation to the structure or to the wall covering, as whether or not a repair is needed. Note if it is "Cosmetic" after you mention the crack, if you think it's ok. On an old house, push on the wall near a window to see if it gives, if you suspect deterioration or termite damage. Bowed paneling on a wall alerts you to moisture or possible water intrusion. Faint water signs can sometimes be found under windows and along the baseboard. Black flash marks on or around an outlet on the wall should be noted. Recommend a licensed electrical contractor inspect further. EXTERIOR: Circle the house slowly paying special attention behind shrubs or hard to reach areas. Check for loose or lifted nails, deterioration, paint peel, caulking at seams, joints, trim, along top of garage door and window brick mold. Swelling of composite siding with recessed nails, green alga areas. Ground clearance of six inches or better where possible is recommended.

II-2027FE25-661D-45B3-8CE2-F5754149E1A3.title: ROOF STRUCTURE AND ATTIC (report leak signs or condensation)
II-2027FE25-661D-45B3-8CE2-F5754149E1A3.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Note any stains around chimney or vent pipes in attic. Is there mold or moisture present?

2. Is there any loose wiring in the attic?

3. Is there any knob and tube wiring in the attic? They should not be covered with insulation.

4. Are the bath and range exhaust fans venting to the outside air?

5. Is there a whole house fan or a thermostatically controlled fan in attic?

6. Is there an air handler in attic? Filter? Drip pan? Float switch obstructed in drip pan?

7. Is insulation installed right side up? (Paper side faces the heated space)

8. Are pull-down stairs to the attic mounted properly to ceiling joists at hinge points? Are nuts tight at each step?

9. Does attic access fit the opening or seal opening properly?

10. Note the absence (or condition) of firewall separation in attic when building is multi-family.

11. Are plywood clips missing between sheets of plywood (if sags are apparent)?

12. Is there any loose wiring or exposed splices at the whole house fan?

13. Note any catch pans or containers in the attic that may indicate periodic leaks

14. Note if rafters are 2 x 4 but not truss construction. Usually found in some older homes and can allow sagging of roof.

More Info:

  • Take your time and trace out the rafters with your light. Move around in all areas accessible. The area you don't check, is the area you missed. Don't miss anything. It pays to have a good flashlight and a back up.
  • Always note fire damage in the attic. And do a stab test to determine the strength. Sometimes the "Char" is only skin deep and it looks worse than it is. If you think it's strong, say so. If not, then recommend an engineer and repairs.
  • Sags can occur where:
    • a plywood clip is missing,
    • a truss is damaged,
    • rafters are spaced too far apart,
    • there is a bad crown in the wood or
    • you have a weak piece of plywood.
  • Undersized wood such as a "2 x 4 rafter" spanned too far can create sag. A knee wall or reinforcement would be suggested.
  • This is also a good time to spot wet signs on insulation to alert you of a possible leak. Also scan for wiring splices and exhaust fan ventilation as well as clearance of insulation around recessed "can" lights.
  • The chimney area often shows stains on wood from previously failed flashing orfrom current. indirect light seen at flashing is sometimes not where it is leaking.
  • Ridge line can show leaks where blow-in occurred or from faulty seams or from end caps being missing.
  • This is a good time to trace out the ceiling exhaust fan vent pipes where possible.

Reference Materials:

II-205BBBF6-7DE5-4B1D-878E-8B690506F5C3.title: VEGETATION, GRADING, DRAINAGE, DRIVEWAYS, PATIO FLOOR, WALKWAYS AND RETAINING WALLS (With respect to their effect on the condition of the building)
II-205BBBF6-7DE5-4B1D-878E-8B690506F5C3.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is there any standing water, poor or negative drainage around the home?

2. Are there any dead trees in the yard?

3. Are there any neighbor infringements noticeable?

4. Are there any signs on the retaining wall or nearby structures that shows difficulty of vehicles backing out of the garage to access the main road?

More Info:

  1. Be sure and comment on any negative slope towards the home that may cause problems like erosion, water intrusion and silt travel. Recommend landscaping or ground cover, vegetation or a retaining wall.
  2. Sometimes a swale, trench or burm created between dirt bank and house (or above dirt bank) may help in diverting water.
  3. A walk around the home dedicated to looking for negative drainage is recommended.

Reference Materials:

II-20B5AC3D-6942-41F0-83D4-9AB92B31032D.title: ROOF DRAINAGE SYSTEMS
II-20B5AC3D-6942-41F0-83D4-9AB92B31032D.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Note any old downspout drain tile/ piping that may no longer work properly or downspouts that need drainlines or splashblocks.

2. Look for where gutters are draining to and if there is standing water in the vicinity. Are there gutter screens installed? Are there leak signs at the gutter seams?

More Info:

  1. Be sure and comment on any negative slope towards building that may cause problems like erosion, water intrusion and silt travel.
  2. Recommend landscaping or ground cover, vegetation or a retaining wall.
  3. Sometimes a swale, trench or burm created between a dirt bank and the house (or above dirt bank) may help in diverting water.
  4. Sometimes a loose or sagging gutter is because long gutter nails have splintered through fascia and missed the rafter tail, or the rafter tail or fascia is deteriorated.
  5. I have recommended in a report that "gutters are loose and needs securing" only to get a call back saying that the rafter tails were deteriorated. While it is impossible for the inspector to check for that without repairing the loose gutter, the buyer should be made aware of the possibility that the gutters are loose because of possible deterioration. It could be as simple as some nails need replacing.

Reference Materials:

II-21F228E6-6A15-4602-9A21-14B1AAB711C9.title: DOORS (REPRESENTATIVE NUMBER)
II-21F228E6-6A15-4602-9A21-14B1AAB711C9.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Found mostly in bathrooms...Does the door open against a wall mounted heater that can cause a fire hazard?

2. Are doorstops or hingestops present?

3. Do doors close and latch properly?

4. Check the closet bi-fold door hardware and note whether or not the doors operate properly

More Info:

  1. All doors should latch when closed and note if the jamb rubs, because seasonal change may make the door swell and have difficulty closing.
  2. Note missing hardware, doorstop, damage etc.
  3. Check bi-folds at the top hardware location for damage.
  4. It is common for bi-folds to need adjustment. Failing to note this can sometimes create a phone call from the buyer, complaining about the bi-fold doors. Sometimes the opening for a bi-fold door needs adjustment which could be significant cosmetic work to correct the opening.

Reference Materials:

II-22C8315F-80A4-42B9-94FB-C852879E9D22.title: WINDOWS
II-22C8315F-80A4-42B9-94FB-C852879E9D22.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is there any staining or discoloration that warrants a finger pressure test on window sills?

More Info:

Unlock window, raise bottom sash fully, then lower to half open and 1/3 open, then close and lock. Note if:

  1. The window won't stay up.
  2. It is difficult to operate.
  3. Check glass, screen, wood casing and trim. The window that you don't inspect is the one that is not working. (Murphy's law).
  4. The window that has all the cute glass knick-knacks on it is the one that doesn't work. (Murphy's law).
  5. Plastic or vinyl windows on a new home can sometimes be extremely difficult to lock. This is because either the window was not installed in the opening correctly (too tight or out of square) which can be a costly issue to correct if it involves removal and re-setting the window, or it is the window itself. According to one manufacturer, newly installed plastic or vinyl windows need to be locked for long periods of time in order for the vinyl to stretch or conform. If left unlocked it can be difficult to line up and lock.
  6. Something else to be alert for when inspecting windows in New Construction is looking for windows that were installed in too wide of an opening. Sometimes daylight can be seen (air infiltration) between the window and side jambs. This could involve a lot of work to correct.

Reference Materials:

II-2546AF74-E8F0-47BC-B3F9-668FBD2059DB.title: MAIN WATER SHUT-OFF DEVICE
II-2546AF74-E8F0-47BC-B3F9-668FBD2059DB.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

More Info:

  1. It is important to tell the client where their main water shut off is and if there is not one, where it can be accessed easily.
  2. If you don't find a main shutoff in the house, then see if the water meter outside and a "street key" is more accessible.
  3. Perhaps a plumber may need to create one for easier access. (In the crawlspace on the front wall is not an easy access.)
  4. You should see if the knob can be turned easily. Sometimes the knob is there but rust or age prevents it from turning.

Reference Materials:

II-26E260CC-D90F-4C9C-9725-79227CEE2FEF.title: FOOD WASTE DISPOSER
II-26E260CC-D90F-4C9C-9725-79227CEE2FEF.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is the disposer wiring missing romex connectors?

2. Is there a loose wiring splice?

3. Is there any loose wiring under the sink where the disposer used to be?

4. If the power switch to the disposal is below a countertop, a child could inadvertently turn it on

More Info:

  1. Check wiring and the romex connector.
  2. Check the drain and sink mount.
  3. Use a flashlight to inspect blades for rust or obstruction. Note if the rubber strainer/shield is worn out.
  4. Run water and turn on disposer. Turn water off and listen to the disposer and note if it is noisy, obstructed etc.
  5. Rusted blades usually means dull blades or perhaps replacement.

Reference Materials:

II-28FB8947-FA49-40A3-AE78-527ECE3209A3.title: INTERIOR WATER SUPPLY AND DISTRIBUTION SYSTEMS AND FIXTURES
II-28FB8947-FA49-40A3-AE78-527ECE3209A3.helpHtml: The home inspector shall observe: Interior water supply and distribution system, including: piping materials, supports, and insulation; fixtures and faucets; functional flow; leaks; and cross connections; Interior drain, waste, and vent system, including: traps; drain, waste, and vent piping; piping supports and pipe insulation; leaks; and functional drainage; Hot water systems including: water heating equipment; normal operating controls; automatic safety controls; and chimneys, flues, and vents; Fuel storage and distribution systems including: interior fuel storage equipment, supply piping, venting, and supports; leaks; and Sump pumps.The home inspector shall describe: Water supply and distribution piping materials; Drain, waste, and vent piping materials; Water heating equipment; and Location of main water supply shutoff device. The home inspector shall operate all plumbing fixtures, including their faucets and all exterior faucets attached to the house, except where the flow end of the faucet is connected to an appliance.The home inspector is not required to: State the effectiveness of anti-siphon devices; Determine whether water supply and waste disposal systems are public or private; Operate automatic safety controls; Operate any valve except water closet flush valves, fixture faucets, and hose faucets; Observe: Water conditioning systems; Fire and lawn sprinkler systems; On-site water supply quantity and quality; On-site waste disposal systems; Foundation irrigation systems; Spas, except as to functional flow and functional drainage; Swimming pools; Solar water heating equipment; or Observe the system for proper sizing, design, or use of proper materials.

II-294D1BB8-26DB-4EFD-AF9B-EECC2A892B21.title: GARAGE FLOOR
II-294D1BB8-26DB-4EFD-AF9B-EECC2A892B21.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Do you have a clear view to inspect all areas in the Garage? Write up and take a picture of areas obstructed because of personal items.

2. Note any settlement cracks in garage floor.

3. Inspect the floor under window locations?

More Info:

  1. Look at an old home with an old eye.
  2. Always note water stains.
  3. On newer homes, note nail pops, exposed or loose sheetrock tape and repair signs.
  4. Workmanship is important in all homes but especially new ones.
  5. Look for signs of only one coat of paint, poor sanding, nail indentations etc.
  6. Look at the perimeter of floor for water stains or deterioration.
  7. Note any areas damaged on floor covering, including stains, exposed seams, small tears or blemishes etc.

ReferenceMaterials:

II-2AB04A20-4E71-42CB-A1DE-0D44CFEA758E.title: RANGES/OVENS/COOKTOPS
II-2AB04A20-4E71-42CB-A1DE-0D44CFEA758E.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Are the support clips in place for the baking or broiler elements in the oven?

2. Are the control knobs legible on the range and do they work properly?

3. Are the grease filters in place and clean for the range fan?

More Info:

  1. First, turn on the broiler in the oven while touching the element, turn off and check the bake element.
  2. Then check the support clips that hold the broiler and bake elements in place, to make sure they're not missing or loose.
  3. Check the oven door for warping and inspect the gasket seal.
  4. Check for burn marks on the oven door frame and for heat loss from a failed gasket and door alignment and springs.
  5. Open and close the storage drawer and check for proper operation.
  6. Turn on all the burners to high, turn back off and finger touch. This method works, and you don't have the risk of someone in the building getting burned while elements are cooling down from the high setting.
  7. On Gas stoves check all burners for even flame at all settings.
  8. Recommend cleaning if a burner delays ignition or if flames pop or if they are uneven.

Reference Materials:

II-2BBC7E1A-C39D-42A8-AE95-F47E17F6FF1C.title: DISTRIBUTION SYSTEMS (including fans, pumps, ducts and piping, with supports, insulation, air filters, registers, radiators, fan coil units and convectors)
II-2BBC7E1A-C39D-42A8-AE95-F47E17F6FF1C.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Inspect the filter condition and look for a poor seal around the filter door or compartment.

2. Is there damaged or loose ductwork, duct tape?

3. Does the furnace or airhandler shut off when the blower door is removed (safety switch)?

4. Note any possible asbestos on old boilers, radiator piping or vent pipe to chimney (older homes). Sometimes asbestos can be found on the underside of decorative radiator covers inside building.

More Info:

  1. Make sure you note if a room does not have a register or vent.
  2. Also inspect all ductwork accessible.
  3. Note if the ductwork is not insulated, if there is AC.
  4. Many times the tape is failing and the ductpipe has pulled loose from the register underneath the floor.
  5. Pull out or examine the filter as part of your air handler inspection. Many times the filter is the wrong size or clogged beyond belief. A clogged filter can cause $10 a month in electricity cost and shorten the life of the unit, not to mention poor air quality.
  6. New construction: Make sure you try to look deep inside the return air cavity in the wall to look for unhealthy items left behind by sub contractors.
  7. Radiators for old boilers can clog or not heat fully. Sometimes they can be blown clean by a boiler technician and sometimes they cannot. One radiator could cost $1000 or more easily ($80 a rung so I've heard) so be sure and write up any that do not get hot on both ends as needing servicing or further inspection by a Boiler technician.
  8. Read the auto-comments in the heat section.

Reference Materials:

II-2E599653-6B97-481E-902A-1D20C81E1232.title: WALLS
II-2E599653-6B97-481E-902A-1D20C81E1232.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Check for firewall separation when the garage wall is integral with another unit/condo.

2. Do you have a clear view to inspect all areas in the Garage?

3. Check the garage wall for vehicle damage or material knocked loose at the soleplate.

4. Check the wall behind the refrigerator for mold?

(Bath)

5. Did you knock on the wall tile at the bath surround to check for loose tile?

6. Did you note loose or missing grout?

7. Is there improper caulk instead of grout and seal?

8. Are there loose, damaged or missing wall accessories such as a towel bar, etc?

9. Is the grab bar inside the tub surround loose?

10. Look for bowed paneling in the lower level or basement, which would be typical of a room with higher moisture levels than the rest of home.

More Info:

  1. Black flash marks on or around an outlet on the wall should be noted.
  2. Understand the difficulties of removing old wall paper.
  3. Note areas where there are bedded nails, and seams where they were not sanded down smooth before painting.
  4. Understand that some walls have oil based paint on them andall buyers are planning to use latex which means their paint job will fail.
  5. Oil can go over oil based or latex. Latex cannot go over oil based paint.
  6. There is a product that is a sealer/primer that would need to go over oil based paint and then latex can be applied.

Reference Materials:

II-2F8C0101-A3ED-4541-8069-AFB22BAF2444.title: SURFACE WALLS AND FLOOR OF POOL

II-31363CE4-FDAE-4C4E-B535-ED48C02340CE.title: SOLID FUEL HEATING DEVICES (Fireplaces, Woodstove)
II-31363CE4-FDAE-4C4E-B535-ED48C02340CE.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Note if the damper is missing or if the lid does not shut off the air completely.

2. Note if the log starter is being improperly used with firelogs (no safety features).

More Info:

  1. Fireplaces: look for damaged or deteriorated fire brick on fire box walls.
  2. Make sure ash dump on the floor of the firebox has a proper lid and a tight seal.
  3. Make sure the damper works and whether or not it is easy to operate.
  4. Looking up into the fireplace, make sure you see no cavity between the finished wall and masonry.
  5. You should see no visible wood or framing.
  6. Be on alert for gas log starters and educate the buyer about the dangers of gas key.
  7. Remember that the match flame should be lit and at the pilot hole before you turn the gas valve when using a key. If not, you wont have any hair left.
  8. My opinion on gas log starters comes from continuing ed and they are dangerous to the homeowner and to a child or teen. They also take awhile to burn solid wood and more creosote is created than with kiln.

Reference Materials:

II-32EA62A5-9DEE-4895-945E-4326CAEFE71F.title: WATER SUPPLY SYSTEM AND FIXTURES
II-32EA62A5-9DEE-4895-945E-4326CAEFE71F.helpHtml: This question is good for miscellaneous plumbing items or components such as pressure reducing valves, broken plumbing, incorrect or problem in plumbing. Outside faucets. To inspect thoroughly, do the basement or crawlspace last. By testing the faucets and drains first (inside the house) will allow you to discover leaks underneath. Trace all plumbing lines and look at the floor or plastic on floor for water or stains etc. Now's a good time to check for a P trap on the washing machine drain line. Also the Dryer vent piping.

II-3351E2CB-2887-4907-A62E-D6434CD1BB07.title: DO STEPS OR LADDERS EXIST ON BOTH SIDES OF THE POOL

II-33D39FC1-06FF-418F-944E-D9D87C426E93.title: VENTING SYSTEMS IN THIS UNIT (Kitchens, baths and laundry if applicable)
II-33D39FC1-06FF-418F-944E-D9D87C426E93.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Do you see where the dryer vent terminates outside?

2. The clothes dryer must vent to outside air. Note if there is a lint trap kit installed instead of venting to the outside air.

3. A gas powered dryer should not use a vinyl ventpipe.

4. A bathroom needs a window or a vent fan.

More Info:

  1. Almost everyone expects an electric 220-volt connection for the Dryer.
  2. Make a note if the only connection for dryer is gas.
  3. Note if both are available, as a plus.
  4. Try to inspect the vent pipe for exhaust fans in the attic to see if they terminate outside.

Reference Materials:

II-3553D62F-6B2E-4766-9DEF-AC7A17FB465D.title: WINDOWS
II-3553D62F-6B2E-4766-9DEF-AC7A17FB465D.helpHtml: Unlock the window, raise the bottom sash fully, then lower to half open and 1/3 open, then close and lock. Note if the window won't stay up or if it is difficult to operate. Check glass, screen, wood casing, trim (check all windows) and Comments.

II-356FCECD-BA59-4088-A4D3-422653BD5530.title: OCCUPANT DOOR FROM GARAGE TO INSIDE HOME
II-356FCECD-BA59-4088-A4D3-422653BD5530.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Note if door does not afford protection such as a fire rated door.

More Info:
