II-35798727-2972-4B06-A8F4-D841F30E8478.title: HOT WATER SYSTEMS, CONTROLS, CHIMNEYS, FLUES AND VENTS
II-35798727-2972-4B06-A8F4-D841F30E8478.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is the gas water heater 18" off the floor and mounted on a proper stand or support?

2. Is the water heater strapped securely to the wall (required in earthquake zones)?

3. If the gas line to the water heater or furnace could be bumped or ruptured by a vehicle, a pole or guard post should be recommended

4. If the water heater is in the crawlspace or basement, it should not be lower than ground level. You may not dig a hole to set the water heater in.

5. Use a lighter at the draft hood when the gas water heater is on to check for proper draw.

6. A gas water heater in the closet needs fresh air from the attic at the ceiling and near the floor.

More Info:

  1. Inspect the plumbing connections and tank housing.
  2. Note rust signs from moisture or condensation (if in a damp area of home) or possible leak at the liner.
  3. Rust along the bottom can be caused when water leaks out while changing heating elements. Sometimes it's hard to distinguish. If you discover rust along the bottom, then remove panel access and feel the insulation to determine if it's currently wet.
  4. Water heaters installed in a crawlspace should not be below ground level.
  5. Gas water heaters installed in a garage should be at least 18 inches off the ground.
  6. When two gas vent pipes enter the chimney together, the highest BTU should enter chimney under the smaller BTU.
  7. Gas water heaters should have the thermostat turned up to force it to come on in order to test the draw at the diverter with a match or lighter. If the draw does not noticeably suck in flame on a match, there could be a venting problem.
  8. White deposits and rust on metal vent pipe can occur from moisture in the gas when not venting properly.
  9. A greasy residue on top of the gas water heater is also a sign of a vent problem.
  10. A blackened or smoky appearance on and around the housing near the flame of a gas water heater indicates the need for more air (combustion air).
  11. The T&P valve (Test and Pressure or Pop off valve) can look fine if the home has not had the water heater on 24 hours before inspection. It can then leak after the buyer moves in. The primary reason is that pressure on the system builds up at night when no one is using water. With gas, the added pressure is a result of steam. Be aware of this when you inspect a vacant home and the water heater has not been on for 24 hours prior.

Reference Materials:

II-361B193B-EA0A-4A92-8BD0-31F39669E34F.title: INTERIOR DRAIN, WASTE AND VENT SYSTEMS
II-361B193B-EA0A-4A92-8BD0-31F39669E34F.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1.(New home) Did you fill sink basins full of water and drain simultaneously to check for leaks at the basket strainer or waster line connections?

2.(Sinks) Is the waste line a P-trap? Is is vented? Are there shut-off valves under the sink?

3. Did you pull back insulation under the bathroom floors to check for leaks or deterioration?

4. Note any temporary repairs to waste lines which include caulking, putty, or homeowner repairs using clamps or flexible piping.

5. Rusted metal waste lines can sometimes collapse or fail upon touching them during inspection.

6. If the washing machine drain line is 1 1/2 inch (older), instead of 2 inch then note the possibility that newer washing machines may overflow a smaller drain (2 inch diameter recommended).

More Info:

  1. Make sure the waste line for plumbing has a trap and vent.
  2. Many older homes still have a 1 1/2" diameter waste line and new washing machines have stronger pumps that may overflow the drain. Not all but some. Look for signs on the wall or floor, or the drain hose may have been modified in some way.
  3. "Gray water" is a term that means that the water drains into the yard and not the sewer or septic system. This could be a violation in your area. Consult with the health department or building safety department on this issue.
  4. Some septic tanks were not designed for the volume of water from a washing machine and could clog if gray water was connected to it. If you discover gray water use, note the possibilities.
  5. The outlet for the washing machine should be grounded. A repair would be to install a GFCI outlet.
  6. Old cast iron waste lines often ooze a leak at pipe connections because the old seals in between pipe connections are deteriorating. It will still work but may need repair. Plumbers who repair these old pipes do not like to repair only one connection, because working on these old pipes can cause other joint connections nearby to fail (hammering, vibration etc.). They will sometimes explain the cost and that it usually includes a larger section for replacement.
  7. The crud that builds up on the inside of these pipes is surprising. That's why sometimes a home plumbing system could work fine until left vacant for 3 -6 months and then the crud inside the pipes begin to dry and fall down and clog pipes. Same is true for old galvanized supply lines when left vacant for long periods. Not always the case but more often than you would think.

Reference Materials:

The home inspector shall observe: Interior water supply and distribution system, including: piping materials, supports, and insulation; fixtures and faucets; functional flow; leaks; and cross connections; Interior drain, waste, and vent system, including: traps; drain, waste, and vent piping; piping supports and pipe insulation; leaks; and functional drainage; Hot water systems including: water heating equipment; normal operating controls; automatic safety controls; and chimneys, flues, and vents; Fuel storage and distribution systems including: interior fuel storage equipment, supply piping, venting, and supports; leaks; and Sump pumps. The home inspector shall describe: Water supply and distribution piping materials; Drain, waste, and vent piping materials; Water heating equipment; and Location of main water supply shutoff device. The home inspector shall operate all plumbing fixtures, including their faucets and all exterior faucets attached to the house, except where the flow end of the faucet is connected to an appliance.

The home inspector is not required to: State the effectiveness of anti-siphon devices; Determine whether water supply and waste disposal systems are public or private; Operate automatic safety controls; Operate any valve except water closet flush valves, fixture faucets, and hose faucets; Observe: Water conditioning systems; Fire and lawn sprinkler systems; On-site water supply quantity and quality; On-site waste disposal systems; Foundation irrigation systems; Spas, except as to functional flow and functional drainage; Swimming pools; Solar water heating equipment; or Observe the system for proper sizing, design, or use of proper materials.

II-3860C2D8-D35B-4E52-BAD4-6C9F1B197280.title: DOES THE DOOR LATCH HEIGHT AND LOCATION ATTEMPT TO BE REASONABLY DIFFICULT FOR YOUNG CHILDREN TO REACH

II-395B5DAA-3D57-4ADD-BA2F-A0C153BDC575.title: COOLING AND AIR HANDLER EQUIPMENT
II-395B5DAA-3D57-4ADD-BA2F-A0C153BDC575.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is the heat pump / condenser level?

2. Are the foam sleeves on the suction line intact?

3. Are bushes or a fence obstructing air flow?

More Info:

Reference Materials:

The home inspector shall observe: Central air conditioning systems including: Cooling and air handling equipment; and Normal operating controls. Distribution systems including: Fans, pumps, ducts and piping, with associated supports, dampers, insulation, air filters, registers, fan-coil units; and The presence of an installed cooling source in each room. The home inspector shall describe: Energy sources; and Cooling equipment type. The home inspector shall operate the systems using normal operating controls. The home inspector shall open readily openable access panels provided by the manufacturer or installer for routine homeowner maintenance

The home inspector is not required to:Operate cooling systems when weather conditions or other circumstances may cause equipment damage; Observe non-central air conditioners; or Observe the uniformity or adequacy of cool-air supply to the various rooms. Ambient air test is when you stick two meat thermometers into the main plenum of the air handler. One in the return air and one in the supply. Preferably near each other at the main trunk. If the AC has been running for an adequate amount of time before test you should see a range somewhere between 14 and 22 degrees. The supply should be the colder of the two. This test is not conclusive because of varying conditions but if it's out of range and the AC has had time to cool the home, then you can recommend an HVAC person (Heating Ventilation and Air Conditioning)

II-39843CBB-2CC9-449D-934A-F458D472640A.title: VERIFY THE ELECTRICAL OUTLET(S) AND ANY LIGHTING FOR POOL IS ON A GROUND FAULT CIRCUIT (GFCI)

II-39A44C76-8B7B-4AF0-802F-0E312D969D72.title: FLOORS (Structural)
II-39A44C76-8B7B-4AF0-802F-0E312D969D72.helpHtml: Look at an old home with an old eye. Always note water stains and whether or not you can determine how old they are by a moisture meter, examining the area related in attic and on roof. Newer homes note nail pops, exposed or loose sheetrock tape and repair signs. Workmanship is important on all homes but especially new ones. Look for signs of only one coat of paint or poor sanding, nail indentations etc. Look at perimeter of floor for water stains or deterioration. Bounce around a little on the floor (without lifting your feet). Note any areas damaged on floor covering, including stains, exposed seams, small tear or blemish etc. See Discoveries and Comments

II-39EE2E65-DC16-42FF-BE1B-02C5A900405F.title: PRESENCE OF INSTALLED HEAT SOURCE IN EACH ROOM
II-39EE2E65-DC16-42FF-BE1B-02C5A900405F.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

More Info:

  1. Don't miss the absence of a vent in a room or you could be sued and be liable for the cost to put one in.
  2. One must also consider: Why isn't one there? It could be the size of the heat/AC unit which would require a bigger unit or perhaps there is no physical way to install one. Extreme remodeling may be involved.
  3. Also, stay alert for the type of heating system in the house with an AC condenser. If it's boiler heat and there is an AC unit outside, and the house is 2 story, it is likely that the AC serves the upstairs only. Therefore it is necessary to point this out in your report.

Reference Materials:

II-3ABD3E85-0888-41A6-BED1-F416C1E23271.title: CEILINGS (structural)
II-3ABD3E85-0888-41A6-BED1-F416C1E23271.helpHtml:
Quick Check:


1. Use the auto comment when ceiling is not visible which is almost always:

Auto Comment:
Most of the walls and ceilings in the finished basement are covered and structural members are not visible. No obvious problems discovered. I could not see behind these coverings.

More Info:

Reference Materials:

II-3C958277-02F5-4E1E-8786-6743762BF23C.title: POLARITY AND GROUNDING OF RECEPTACLES WITHIN 6 FEET OF INTERIOR PLUMBING FIXTURES, AND ALL RECEPTACLES IN GARAGE, CARPORT,  EXTERIOR WALLS OF INSPECTED STRUCTURE
II-3C958277-02F5-4E1E-8786-6743762BF23C.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Do you notice any GFCI outlets with freezers plugged into them? Don't forget to reset GFCI. Two prong plugs in the Garage or around any areas with water?

More Info:

  1. I use a simple three-prong plug with a GFCI test button. It identifies whether or not the outlet is grounded, and if the polarity is correct.
  2. Some tips are: Your three-prong GFCI test plug will not "trip" the outlet if it is a non-grounded GFCI. But it still should trip by pressing the test button on outlet, and kill the circuit.
  3. A non-grounded outlet can be corrected by either attaching a ground wire to the outlet and attach it to a metal rod or a metal plumbing pipe.
  4. Or, replace the three-prongnon-grounded outlet with a three-prong GFCI outlet. A sticker should be on the outlet that identifies it as non-grounded.
  5. Or last, change the circuit breaker to a GFCI breaker at the panel.
  6. You can "trip" a non-grounded GFCI with a voltmeter by placing one prong of the voltmeter in the short slit of the outlet, and take the other prong of the voltmeter and touch a metal plumbing pipe (that eventually contacts the soil).
  7. Most three-prong GFCI plugs will show two lights at the end of the plug when the outlet being tested is grounded. When you press the button on the plug, both lights should remain lit and strong. If however, the plug lights up only one of the two grounding lights "Faint or Dim" and you press the button on the plug and it shows "Reverse polarity", it may just be a "loose" ground wire and can be corrected a lot easier than having to install a new ground wire.
  8. Just because you can press the test button on the GFCI outlet using your finger and it "trips," doesn't mean it killed the circuit. It could be defective.
  9. New GFCI outlets can be defective when installed.
  10. Always use the three-prong GFCI test plug on every three-prong outlet.
  11. Homeowners frequently use a freezer in their garage. Most outlets in the garage are on a GFCI Circuit. When you're inspecting the home don't forget to reset the GFCI outlet or you may be buying the homeowners spoiled food.

Reference Materials:

II-3CFF6FAA-29C4-4483-BC15-23F2BDB2606B.title: ARE THERE ANY OBSTRUCTIONS (WALLS, SHRUBS etc.) THAT WOULD PREVENT FULL VIEW OF POOL FROM HOME

II-3D99255C-5317-4AD0-82A2-B8555D9EC636.title: CEILINGS
II-3D99255C-5317-4AD0-82A2-B8555D9EC636.helpHtml: Look at an old home with an old eye. Always note water stains and whether or not you can determine how old they are by a moisture meter, examining the area related in attic and on roof. Newer homes note nail pops, exposed or loose sheetrock tape and repair signs. Workmanship is important on all homes but especially new ones. Look for signs of only one coat of paint or poor sanding, nail indentations etc. Look at perimeter of floor for water stains or deterioration. Bounce around a little on the floor (without lifting your feet). Note any areas damaged on floor covering, including stains, exposed seams, small tear or blemish etc. See Discoveries and Comments

II-3F20B822-8583-4CBB-B37D-0F791365F245.title: SKYLIGHTS, CHIMNEYS AND ROOF PENETRATIONS
II-3F20B822-8583-4CBB-B37D-0F791365F245.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Does the vent pipe boot/flange on roof fit snug around the pipe?

2. Inspect the chimney above the roofline for Spalling, cracks, missing mortar or missing rain cap.

3. Inspect the chimney crown and note any cracked or missing mortar, or improper caulking or silicone in cracks that may fail.

4. Do ridge vents have end caps and nail heads caulked? Are passive vents flashed properly? Do turbines turn freely?

5. Does the skylight have a flash kit or was it homemade? Are there repair/caulk signs? Cloudy appearance?

6. Is chimney leaning or are there signs of trim rework where chimney contacts the wall of home?

More Info:

  1. Skylights without manufactured flash kits can leak a lot easier than properly installed flash kits.
  2. Skylights can go for years with no problems and leak only after time has passed and for no apparent reason noticed.
  3. Skylights can leak on one rainy day and not leak on another. It is impossible to look at a skylight installation and know if it will leak or not. Even when it looks perfect.
  4. Homes that have had a pressure washing company spray onto skylights can blow away, or push sealant caulking away, and cause leaks. You can't know what has happened since the skylight has been installed.
  5. Look for fresh paint inside at the skylight chase or tell-tale water marks that may only be condensation and not leaks.
  6. Vaulted ceilings with skylights can cause condensation in summer, if the ceiling air gets hot enough and an AC vent is mixing with hot ceiling air. Water droplets (or stains) can form on the ceiling. Sometimes it is difficult to determine which one is occurring in the home.
  7. Chimneys: Look for loose mortar above the roof line.
  8. Check the cement crown for cracks.
  9. White efflorescence or flaking of brick (spalling) indicates moisture is soaking into the brick somewhere.
  10. Do not try to remove metal hood bonnets on chimney to inspect liner. They sometimes are difficult to get back on or have been semi-permanently glued requiring a lot of work each time it is removed.
  11. Wood siding chimneys can deteriorate if metal hood does not completely cover outside corner boards.
  12. Stucco peeling away from the surface it is bonded to, is generally caused from moisture or a previously painted sub surface (painted masonry block that stucco is applied on).
  13. Brick divider walls separating flues are still found on many old homes. Loose or missing brick in these divider walls calls for a certified chimney sweep to inspect further.
  14. Roof penetrations: Know how to flash a chimney, install a vent pipe or vent fan hood flange into the weave of shingles.

Reference Materials:

II-3F4C2BC7-F26C-41BF-A5F1-9B04E49BBD89.title: ATTIC INSULATION
II-3F4C2BC7-F26C-41BF-A5F1-9B04E49BBD89.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is insulation right side up? (Paper side faces the heated space).

2. Is there any loose, missing or hanging insulation?

More Info:

  1. To get R-Value for Fiberglass, Rock Wool and Mineral Fiber, multiply the thickness in inches by 3.142857.
  2. For Cellulose, multiply inches by 3.6666 to find R-Value.
  3. Insulation usually comes in four types: Loose-fill, Batts, Rolls and Rigid Foam Board.
  4. Fiberglass is recycled glass and sand
  5. Rock Wool is recycled Steel scraps and Basaltic Rock
  6. Cellulose is recycled newspapers treated with fire retardant chemicals (Borax).
  7. Rigid Foam Board (used on exterior side of walls and behind the ceiling panel of a Cathedral ceiling) obviously not visible or accessible during an inspection.
  8. A building can lose 50% of it's heat through the roof, with 25% going through the walls and windows, and 25% through the floor.

A rough guess of R value in the attic is determined by the thickness of insulation:

  1. about 6 inches thick or just under 22 R value
  2. about 7 inches thick or 25.6 R-value
  3. about 8 inches thick or just over 29 R-value
  4. about 9 inches thick or just under 33 R-value
  5. about 10 inches thick or just over 36.6 R-value
  6. about 11 inches thick or just over 40 R-value
  7. about 12 inches thick or just under 44 R-value
  8. about 13 inches thick or 47.6 R-value
  9. about 14 inches thick or just at 51 R-value
  10. about 15 inches thick or just under 55 R-value
  11. about 16 inches thick or 58 R-value

Reference Materials:

The building inspector shall observe: Insulation and vapor retarders in unfinished spaces; Ventilation of attics and foundation areas; Kitchen, bathroom, and laundry venting systems; and the operation of any readily accessible attic ventilation fan, and, when temperature permits, the operation of any readily accessible thermostatic control. The building inspector shall describe: Insulation in unfinished spaces; and Absence of insulation in unfinished space at conditioned surfaces. The building inspector shall: Move insulation where readily visible evidence indicates the need to do so; and Move insulation where chimneys penetrate roofs, where plumbing drain/waste pipes penetrate floors, adjacent to earth filled stoops or porches, and at exterior doors.

The building inspector is not required to report on: Concealed insulation and vapor retarders; or Venting equipment that is integral with household appliances.

II-3F7C1FE3-6D50-4312-8773-CD692CD8A576.title: VENTILATION OF ATTIC AND FOUNDATION AREAS
II-3F7C1FE3-6D50-4312-8773-CD692CD8A576.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Are there any foundation vents below ground level, without wells, that can allow water intrusion?

More Info:

Reference Materials:

II-4121E702-5646-4B8C-A9A4-78253B5D2A3F.title: WINDOWS (REPRESENTATIVE NUMBER)
II-4121E702-5646-4B8C-A9A4-78253B5D2A3F.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Did you test the windows or write "Not Inspected" when a window has knick-knacks stacked on it?

2. Be sure to note if a window A/C is preventing testing the operation of a window.

3. Are storm windows missing or damaged on single pane windows?

4. Is any weatherstripping missing on windows?

5. Are sash cords missing or replaced with jamb hardware on the windows?

6. Was every accessible window tested for operation? If not, did you note which ones were not tested?

7. Cloudy windows? Note windows that appear cloudy and also note windows that are out of reach and can't be determined if they are cloudy or just dirty.

More Info:

  1. This is where you look for cloudy windows and lock hardware and cracked or loose glass.
  2. Also check the sill for strength against deterioration.
  3. Walls leaking around windows can sometimes be discovered by inspecting the sill for deterioration.

Reference Materials:

II-420102BA-3614-42DA-A53C-399649F44F64.title: DOORS (Exterior)
II-420102BA-3614-42DA-A53C-399649F44F64.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is there any staining or discoloration that warrants a finger pressure test on exterior door trim /jambs at bottom (including sliding glass doors, patio doors, side lights etc.)?

2. Note if the main entry doors are hollow core which is not as secure as a solid core.

3. Does the garage door opening height and width seem normal?

4. The garage door must reverse when met with resistance regardless of whether or not they have sensors. Sensors should be no higher off the floor than 6" or according to manufacturer specs.

5. What is the condition of the weather-stripping at garage door floor and sides?

6. Check both sides of Garage door for damage?

7. The "jerk and let go" test for the garage door works best but there is a risk of damaging the door if you don't let go quick enough. A 2 x 4 block placed on floor can damage a metal door if door does not reverse (not recommended).

8. Note older garage door springs that do not have retention cables to contain the spring if the cable breaks.

More Info:

  1. Always open and shut a door from both sides and note whether or not the door latches.
  2. Also note if the door is out of square enough that it no longer ensures privacy.
  3. Check for holes in doors and for a doorstop on each one. Note any trim or hardware missing (check all doors).
  4. Basement or Crawlspace: Make sure that the door fits properly and is properly painted. Look at the ground in front of the door for negative slope that may allow water intrusion.
  5. Check to see if the door is delaminating or deteriorated at the bottom .
  6. Sliding glass and patio doors: Open and close doors as needed and check for "daylight" and continuous weather-stripping.
  7. Also, close the door with knob until it latches. Then turn deadbolt and check strike for proper alignment and a tight fit.
  8. Also look carefully at the glass, and check for "Cloudy" appearance or cracked glass. This is a good time to inspect the floor area around door for possible water intrusion or deterioration.
  9. Garage doors: Raise the garage door and lay a 2 x 4 block on the floor at the middle of the door opening (except a metal door that could be damaged by a 2 x 4 block). Document if the door reverses or not.
  10. If you use your hand to provide resistance and the door does not reverse, you can severely damage the door if you're not careful. The door can "fold-up" damaging the door panel and chain drive.
  11. Even if the door has electronic sensors, it still should reverse when met with resistance. Adjustment screws are usually found on the side and rear of opener. These door adjustment screws can be tricky to adjust.

II-420872F8-6A06-475E-8355-C9859183CBFA.helpHtml: Look at an old home with an old eye. Always note water stains and whether or not you can determine how old they are by a moisture meter, examining the area related in attic and on roof. Newer homes note nail pops, exposed or loose sheetrock tape and repair signs. Workmanship is important on all homes but especially new ones. Look for signs of only one coat of paint or poor sanding, nail indentations etc. Look at perimeter of floor for water stains or deterioration. Bounce around a little on the floor (without lifting your feet). Note any areas damaged on floor covering, including stains, exposed seams, small tear or blemish etc. See Discoveries and Comments

II-435F330C-FA66-4AE6-BB6A-1C94651AF19F.title: FOOD WASTE DISPOSER
II-435F330C-FA66-4AE6-BB6A-1C94651AF19F.helpHtml: Check wiring and romex connector. Check drain and sink mount. Use flashlight to inspect blades for rust or obstruction. Note if rubber strainer/shield is worn out. Run water and turn on disposer. Turn water off and listen to the disposer and note if noisy, obstructed etc. Rusted blades usually means dull blades or perhaps replacement.

II-45D69D8D-B77B-48D2-B1FE-65FD1F83CC1A.title: OPERATION OF GFCI  (GROUND FAULT CIRCUIT INTERRUPTERS)
II-45D69D8D-B77B-48D2-B1FE-65FD1F83CC1A.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

More Info:

  1. I use a simple three-prong plug with a GFCI test button. It identifies whether or not the outlet is grounded, and if the polarity is correct.
  2. Some tips are: Your three-prong GFCI test plug will not "trip" the outlet if it is a non-grounded GFCI. But it still should trip by pressing the test button on outlet, and kill the circuit.
  3. A non-grounded outlet can be corrected by either attaching a ground wire to the outlet and attach it to a metal rod or a metal plumbing pipe.
  4. Or, replace the three-prongnon-grounded outlet with a three-prong GFCI outlet. A sticker should be on the outlet that identifies it as non-grounded.
  5. Or last, change the circuit breaker to a GFCI breaker at the panel.
  6. You can "trip" a non-grounded GFCI with a voltmeter by placing one prong of the voltmeter in the short slit of the outlet, and take the other prong of the voltmeter and touch a metal plumbing pipe (that eventually contacts the soil).
  7. Most three-prong GFCI plugs will show two lights at the end of the plug when the outlet being tested is grounded. When you press the button on the plug, both lights should remain lit and strong. If however, the plug lights up only one of the two grounding lights "Faint or Dim" and you press the button on the plug and it shows "Reverse polarity", it may just be a "loose" ground wire and can be corrected a lot easier than having to install a new ground wire.
  8. Just because you can press the test button on the GFCI outlet using your finger and it "trips," doesn't mean it killed the circuit. It could be defective.
  9. New GFCI outlets can be defective when installed.
  10. Always use the three-prong GFCI test plug on every three-prong outlet.
  11. Homeowners frequently use a freezer in their garage. Most outlets in the garage are on a GFCI Circuit. When you're inspecting the home don't forget to reset the GFCI outlet or you may be buying the homeowners spoiled food.

II-46436915-D96C-4D02-B675-4263E0ACB167.title: GARAGE DOOR OPERATORS (Report whether or not doors will reverse when met with resistance)
II-46436915-D96C-4D02-B675-4263E0ACB167.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is the auto-opener using a light fixture adapter or an extension cord that's not approved?

2. Look for a missing cover, burnt cover, missing bulb etc.

3. Look for the electrical plug and make sure it has a proper outlet in reach.

4. Some doors do not reverse when met with resistance and could kill. Always be concerned about that.

5. The reason why the door needs to reverse when met with resistance, even with sensors in place, is because if a truck bed or bumper was extended into the door path and is higher than the sensors, major damage would occur.

6. Doors that need adjustment in order to reverse may not be able to be adjusted. Sometimes the adjustment screws/knobs will not adjust it properly.

7. Check for height to accommodate most vehicles or let them know a large car may not fit.

More Info:

II-49059E58-5FEE-4330-A483-6407F3206F16.title: FLASHINGS
II-49059E58-5FEE-4330-A483-6407F3206F16.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is there a lack of or improper flashing at wall junctions or chimneys?

2. Does dormer siding have sufficient clearance from the roof? Is it flashed properly?

More Info:

  1. Flashings are hidden most of the time, but you can go to the roof and wall junctions and tap on the shingle to see if it flexes away from the flashing underneath.
  2. Know what step flashing is, along with cap or counter flashing. The cap or counter flashing provides a hood over the step flashing and is bent and inserted into a masonry cut groove in brick or block. Flashing a rock chimney after a roof tear off is near impossible to do properly because you can't cut a groove in rock to tuck in bent flashing. The cap flashing is then laid flush and caulked at top, often failing in a short period of time.
  3. There is a product called Peel-n-Seal that is a foil backed sheet of tar and is pliable. It comes in a roll that can be cut with a knife and after peeling off wax paper can be molded to fit and seal against uneven surfaces like rock or stone. Some guys heat up the tar backing first with a butane torch for immediate sealing, depending on outside temperatures. This doesn't look as good as copper, but is a lot better than not installing proper cap or counter flashing.

II-4A7FFA0D-3EA7-492B-AC82-CACA371578AF.title: COOLING AND HEATING EQUIPMENT
II-4A7FFA0D-3EA7-492B-AC82-CACA371578AF.helpHtml:

1. Is the heat pump / condenser level?

2. Are the foam sleeves on the suction line intact?

3. Are bushes or a fence obstructing air flow?

The building inspector shall observe: Central air conditioning systems including: Cooling and air handling equipment; and Normal operating controls. Distribution systems including: Fans, pumps, ducts and piping, with associated supports, dampers, insulation, air filters, registers, fan-coil units; and The presence of an installed cooling source in each room. The building inspector shall describe: Energy sources; and Cooling equipment type. The building inspector shall operate the systems using normal operating controls. The building inspector shall open readily openable access panels provided by the manufacturer or installer for routine homeowner maintenance

The building inspector is not required to:Operate cooling systems when weather conditions or other circumstances may cause equipment damage; Observe non-central air conditioners; or Observe the uniformity or adequacy of cool-air supply to the various rooms. Ambient air test is when you stick two meat thermometers into the main plenum of the air handler. One in the return air and one in the supply. Preferably near each other at the main trunk. If the AC has been running for an adequate amount of time before test you should see a range somewhere between 14 and 22 degrees. The supply should be the colder of the two. This test is not conclusive because of varying conditions but if it's out of range and the AC has had time to cool the building, then you can recommend an HVAC person (Heating Ventilation and Air Conditioning)

II-4BDBA641-A2EF-4158-839D-2CE0836DCE69.title: MICROWAVE COOKING EQUIPMENT
II-4BDBA641-A2EF-4158-839D-2CE0836DCE69.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Anold building with a brand new microwave may trip a circuit breaker, since old homes did not have a separate circuit for the microwave. Check the panel to determine if you can see a new dedicated circuit. If not, write up the possibility.

More Info:

  1. They make a cool microwave tester. You can get them in any inspector tool mag.
  2. Be alert that in older homes, they may have added a microwave to the kitchen's existing circuitry and may be on a shared circuit. Sometimes an older microwave worked fine but a new one can draw more amps and trip the circuit. Microwaves should have their own 20 amp dedicated circuit but in many older homes, they do not.

II-4CD415FB-9285-47E4-9F18-6F5A32227117.title: PLUMBING WATER SUPPLY AND DISTRIBUTION SYSTEMS AND FIXTURES
II-4CD415FB-9285-47E4-9F18-6F5A32227117.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Did you tug on the hose bib(s) and test them for operation?

2. Did you write in the report that you did not remove garden hose to check for a drip?

3. Does the spray nozzle leak or drip above or below the sink when faucet is turned on? Is the aerator working?

4. Does the plumbing system pass the functional flow test? (Run a shower at bathing temperature and then turn on the sink faucets and flush the toilet. If you can still take a shower, it passes).

(Toilets)

5. Does the toilet tank lid fit properly?

6. Does the tank have condensation leaking onto the floor?

7. Is the toilet loose at the floor connection? Are there leak signs?

8. Was the vinyl floor cut around the toilet?

9. Did you check the floor on each side of toilet with your weight?

10. Lift the toilet tank lid and inspect water quality (iron or sediment). Some sellers will attempt to clean or hide iron problems before the inspection but they forget about cleaning inside the toilet tank

(Shower or bathtubs)

11. Are the tub faucets or shower arm loose in the wall when tugged on?

12. Are the hot and cold faucets reversed?

13. Are any bathtubs missing a shower?

14. Are there any corroded galvanized supply lines? Wet joints? Are they supported ok?

15. Old concrete sinks need to be partially filled to check for leaks.

16. Check for poly piping and use auto-comment if poly is present

17. Indicate whether or not the jet powered tub worked properly

More Info:

  1. Be sure to check in several areas throughout your inspection on the type of water supply or distribution materials in the home. Sometimes there are several in one home.
  2. Poly piping has become a concern. The real negative is that some people believe that it is not "if" but "when" the poly will fail. It is estimated that poly will fail within 15 years of installation. Whether this is true or not, it is important for you to know that someone may say that in court for the plaintiff and you might be the defendant. Keep that in mind.
  3. Pex material comes in colors and replaces poly as far as flexibility in installation.
  4. CPVC is easy to install but freeze breaks can split CPVCcausing significant damage. Instead of a small split in the pipe like will happen with copper, CPVC can take out many feet if not all the exposed piping that froze.
  5. Copper seems to be the tried and true choice.
  6. Toilet tanks can tell a lot. I have had sellers with iron problems clean all the brown from all fixtures before inspection and then lift the tank lid and see what they missed. Great time to take a picture.

II-5104204C-E476-4EFF-A28F-67509DD9F1ED.title: RANGES/OVENS/COOKTOPS
II-5104204C-E476-4EFF-A28F-67509DD9F1ED.helpHtml: First, turn on the broiler in oven while touching element, turn off and check the bake element. Then check the support clips that hold the broiler and bake elements in place to make sure they're not missing or loose. Check the oven door for warp and inspect gasket seal. Check for burn marks at the oven doorframe for heat loss from failed gasket or door alignment or springs. Open close storage drawer for proper operation. Turn on all the burners to high, finger touch and turn back off. This method works and you don't have the risk of someone in home getting burned while elements are cooling down from high setting. On Gas stoves check all burners for even flame at all settings. Recommend cleaning if a burner delays ignition or if flames pop or if uneven.

2. Does the door support itself when opened?

3. Are there rusted racks?

4. Is it old or noisy?

5. Does the drain line connect to a wasteline above the trap?

6. Does the drain line perform a loop in the line?

More Info:

The home inspector shall observe and operate the basic functions of the following kitchen appliances: Permanently installed dishwasher, through its normal cycle; Range, cook top, and permanently installed oven; Trash compactor; Garbage disposal; Ventilation equipment or range hood; and Permanently installed microwave oven.

The home inspector is not required to observe: Clocks, timers, self-cleaning oven function, or thermostats for calibration or automatic operation; Non built-in appliances; or Refrigeration units. The home inspector is not required to operate: Appliances in use; or Any appliance that is shut down or otherwise inoperable.

II-5440A874-B7B6-4E22-9ECD-DB80CD36F797.title: GARAGE WALLS (INCLUDING FIREWALL SEPARATION)

2. Do you have a clear view to inspect all areas in the Garage?

3. Check the garage wall for vehicle damage or material knocked loose at the soleplate.

4. Look for bowed paneling which would be typical of a room with higher moisture levels than the rest of home.

More Info:

  1. Black flash marks on or around an outlet on the wall should be noted.
  2. Understand the difficulties of removing old wall paper.
  3. Note areas where there are bedded nails, and seams where they were not sanded down smooth before painting.
  4. Understand that some walls have oil based paint on them andall buyers are planning to use latex which means their paint job will fail.
  5. Oil can go over oil based or latex. Latex cannot go over oil based paint.
  6. There is a product that is a sealer/primer that would need to go over oil based paint and then latex can be applied.

Check the metal ID tag and make sure that the type of fuel at the house matches the type that the logs are designed for (Gas/LP).

Quick Check:

1. Is the heat pump / condenser level?

2. Are the foam sleeves on the suction line intact?

3. Are bushes or a fence obstructing air flow?

4. Hydronic systems should have a water heater that is designed for heating the home and not use converted water heaters. Converted water heaters may not have a high enough BTU rating.

5. Are there any electric outlets located on the wall above the electric baseboard which could be a possible fire hazard?

More Info:

  1. Heating Equipment over 15 years old and still operating should still be noted as old, and recommend servicing them annually to monitor for safe operation.
  2. (Oil furnaces) Check around the sight hole for smoke stains around the collar that may be leaking fumes.
  3. Examine the vent pipe and where it enters chimney for integrity and proper seal.
  4. Check for back drafting by using a lighter or match around joints in the vent pipe, or at an existing test hole (if any).
  5. An erratic movement of the damper lid on the vent pipe and/or soot build-up should be noted.
  6. The furnace should run for at least 15 minutes.
  7. It's a good technique to observe the firing, or ignition, of the furnace. To do this, use the cut-off switch at the furnace before you set the thermostat to turn the furnace on. If it's not running normally, recommend a licensed heat contractor for service and repair as needed.
  8. Learn how to perform a smoke bomb test. Use a Gas Tracer.
  9. ( GAS FURNACES ) Use a gas tracer around the unit. Examine burners and raceway for charred bits and recommend service if bits are excessive or flame is not even.
  10. If flame dances sharply or rolls under the burner recommend service.
  11. Heat exchangers or the steel liner is more likely to crack near the pilot light.
  12. ( BOILERS ) should be tested for 30 to 45 minutes to allow all radiators to heat fully. Some radiators that are old may take longer to heat but you have to decide while your there if they heat from one end to the other. This time is needed to allow pressure to build and check for leaks. Radiators are extremely expensive and you don't want to miss even one. If over 15 years old and operating well it should be noted as old and recommend servicing annually to monitor for safe operation.
  13. Check around the sight hole for smoke stains around the collar that may be leaking fumes. Examine the vent pipe and where it enters the chimney for integrity and proper seal.
  14. Check for back drafting by using a lighter or match around joints in the vent pipe, or at an existing test hole (if any).
  15. Steam boilers have a sight glass to check water level.
  16. Circulating boilers do not have a sight glass.
  17. Boilers should be flushed regularly as part of a normal maintenance schedule.
  18. ( HEAT PUMPS ) should not be ran in AC mode if temp outside is @ 65 degrees or less. You could damage the unit.
  19. Be sure and note if you did not inspect it. Just because you have heat coming out of the registers doesn't mean your compressor outside is working.
  20. The fan outside should be moving. Just because the fan outside is moving doesn't mean you have heat.
  21. Grab the suction line before it enters air handler inside and feel for heat.
  22. In summer, hand check the suction line for ice cold. No cold feeling means recommending service.
  23. The coils inside the air handler may need cleaning or the liquid line may need refrigerant.
  24. Only trouble shooting by a qualified heat contractor can determine exactly.
  25. The ambient air test differential on a heat pump should be between 14 and 22 degrees. Use a thermometer at the main plenum and use one at the return air at the air handler. The difference in these (in AC mode) should be 14 to 22 degrees.
  26. ( ELECTRIC BASE ) should be turned on and checked for proper operation, securely fastened to wall or floor.
  27. There should never be an outlet on the wall directly above electric base.
  28. Remove the front cover on the baseboard and inspect the wire that runs the length of the base located inside a tube. This wire can become brittle or weak over time, and cause abnormal heating up of unit and can cause a fire.

Reference Materials:

The home inspector shall observe permanently installed heating systems including: Heating equipment; Normal operating controls; Automatic safety controls; Chimneys, flues, and vents, where readily visible; Solid fuel heating devices; Heat distribution systems including fans, pumps, ducts and piping, with supports, insulation, air filters, registers, radiators, fan coil units, convectors; and the presence of an installed heat source in each room. The home inspector shall describe: Energy source; and Heating equipment and distribution type. The home inspector shall operate the systems using normal operating controls. The home inspector shall open readily openable access panels provided by the manufacturer or installer for routine homeowner maintenance.

The home inspector is not required to: Operate heating systems when weather conditions or other circumstances may cause equipment damage; Operate automatic safety controls; Ignite or extinguish solid fuel fires; or Observe: The interior of flues; Fireplace insert flue connections; Humidifiers; Electronic air filters; or The uniformity or adequacy of heat supply to the various rooms.

II-5678A63E-37A2-4A49-98C6-19922321409D.title: PLUMBING  DRAIN, WASTE AND VENT SYSTEMS
II-5678A63E-37A2-4A49-98C6-19922321409D.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1.(New home) Did you fill sink basins full of water and drain simultaneously to check for leaks at the basket strainer or waster line connections?

2.(Sinks) Is the waste line a P-trap? Is is vented? Are there shut-off valves under the sink?

3. Did you pull back insulation under the bathroom floors to check for leaks or deterioration?

4. Note any temporary repairs to waste lines which include caulking, putty, or homeowner repairs using clamps or flexible piping.

5. Rusted metal waste lines can sometimes collapse or fail upon touching them during inspection.

6. If the washing machine drain line is 1 1/2 inch (older), instead of 2 inch then note the possibility that newer washing machines may overflow a smaller drain (2 inch diameter recommended).

More Info:

  1. Make sure the waste line for plumbing has a trap and vent.
  2. Many older homes still have a 1 1/2" diameter waste line and new washing machines have stronger pumps that may overflow the drain. Not all but some. Look for signs on the wall or floor, or the drain hose may have been modified in some way.
  3. "Gray water" is a term that means that the water drains into the yard and not the sewer or septic system. This could be a violation in your area. Consult with the health department or building safety department on this issue.
  4. Some septic tanks were not designed for the volume of water from a washing machine and could clog if gray water was connected to it. If you discover gray water use, note the possibilities.
  5. The outlet for the washing machine should be grounded. A repair would be to install a GFCI outlet.
  6. Old cast iron waste lines often ooze a leak at pipe connections because the old seals in between pipe connections are deteriorating. It will still work but may need repair. Plumbers who repair these old pipes do not like to repair only one connection, because working on these old pipes can cause other joint connections nearby to fail (hammering, vibration etc.). They will sometimes explain the cost and that it usually includes a larger section for replacement.
  7. The crud that builds up on the inside of these pipes is surprising. That's why sometimes a home plumbing system could work fine until left vacant for 3 -6 months and then the crud inside the pipes begin to dry and fall down and clog pipes. Same is true for old galvanized supply lines when left vacant for long periods. Not always the case but more often than you would think.

Reference Materials:

The home inspector shall observe: Interior water supply and distribution system, including: piping materials, supports, and insulation; fixtures and faucets; functional flow; leaks; and cross connections; Interior drain, waste, and vent system, including: traps; drain, waste, and vent piping; piping supports and pipe insulation; leaks; and functional drainage; Hot water systems including: water heating equipment; normal operating controls; automatic safety controls; and chimneys, flues, and vents; Fuel storage and distribution systems including: interior fuel storage equipment, supply piping, venting, and supports; leaks; and Sump pumps. The home inspector shall describe: Water supply and distribution piping materials; Drain, waste, and vent piping materials; Water heating equipment; and Location of main water supply shutoff device. The home inspector shall operate all plumbing fixtures, including their faucets and all exterior faucets attached to the house, except where the flow end of the faucet is connected to an appliance.

The home inspector is not required to: State the effectiveness of anti-siphon devices; Determine whether water supply and waste disposal systems are public or private; Operate automatic safety controls; Operate any valve except water closet flush valves, fixture faucets, and hose faucets; Observe: Water conditioning systems; Fire and lawn sprinkler systems; On-site water supply quantity and quality; On-site waste disposal systems; Foundation irrigation systems; Spas, except as to functional flow and functional drainage; Swimming pools; Solar water heating equipment; or Observe the system for proper sizing, design, or use of proper materials.

II-567AE47E-FD2E-44EA-B1FD-2A90384FD8A4.title: GARAGE FLOOR
II-567AE47E-FD2E-44EA-B1FD-2A90384FD8A4.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Do you have a clear view to inspect all areas in the Garage? Write up and take a picture of areas obstructed because of personal items.

2. Note any settlement cracks in garage floor.

3. Inspect the floor under window locations?

More Info:

  1. Look at an old home with an old eye.
  2. Always note water stains.
  3. On newer homes, note nail pops, exposed or loose sheetrock tape and repair signs.
  4. Workmanship is important in all homes but especially new ones.
  5. Look for signs of only one coat of paint, poor sanding, nail indentations etc.
  6. Look at the perimeter of floor for water stains or deterioration.
  7. Note any areas damaged on floor covering, including stains, exposed seams, small tears or blemishes etc.

ReferenceMaterials:

II-58A2795E-B7B1-4A92-855E-F3309A3B4E45.title: DISHWASHER
II-58A2795E-B7B1-4A92-855E-F3309A3B4E45.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is the dishwasher secure to the countertop?

2. Does the door support itself when opened?

3. Are there rusted racks?

4. Is it old or noisy?

5. Does the drain line connect to a wasteline above the trap?

6. Does the drain line perform a loop in the line?

More Info:

Reference Materials:

The building inspector shall observe and operate the basic functions of the following kitchen appliances: Permanently installed dishwasher, through its normal cycle; Range, cook top, and permanently installed oven; Trash compactor; Garbage disposal; Ventilation equipment or range hood; and Permanently installed microwave oven.

The building inspector is not required to observe: Clocks, timers, self-cleaning oven function, or thermostats for calibration or automatic operation; Non built-in appliances; or Refrigeration units. The building inspector is not required to operate: Appliances in use; or Any appliance that is shut down or otherwise inoperable.

II-5B0199D8-81E9-42D8-9F55-A0A7B5702F8B.title: PRESENCE OF INSTALLED HEAT SOURCE IN EACH ROOM
II-5B0199D8-81E9-42D8-9F55-A0A7B5702F8B.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

More Info:

  1. Don't miss the absence of a vent in a room or you could be sued and be liable for the cost to put one in.
  2. One must also consider: Why isn't one there? It could be the size of the heat/AC unit which would require a bigger unit or perhaps there is no physical way to install one. Extreme remodeling may be involved.
  3. Also, stay alert for the type of heating system in the house with an AC condenser. If it's boiler heat and there is an AC unit outside, and the house is 2 story, it is likely that the AC serves the upstairs only. Therefore it is necessary to point this out in your report.

II-5BD2CC16-17B6-4CBF-A704-3E641CC6CD43.title: ROOF STRUCTURE AND ATTIC (If the attic is inaccessible, report the method used to inspect)
II-5BD2CC16-17B6-4CBF-A704-3E641CC6CD43.helpHtml: Take your time and trace out the rafters with your light. Move around in all areas accessible. The area you don't check, is the area you missed something. Don't miss anything. It pays to have a good flashlight and a back up. Always note fire damage in the attic.  And do a stab test to determine the strength of a charred area. Sometimes the"Char" is only skin deep and it looks worse than it is. If you think it's strong, say so. If not, then recommend repairs. Sags can occur where a plywood clip is missing, you have a damaged truss or rafters spaced a little too far apart or you have a bad crown in wood. Or possibly a weak piece of plywood. Undersized wood such as a "2 x 4" rafter spanned too far can create sag. A knee wall or reinforcement would be suggested. This is also a good time to spot wet signs on insulation to alert you of a possible leak. Also scan for wiring splices and exhaust fan ventilation and clearance of insulation around recessed "can" lights. To get the R-Value for Fiberglass, Rock Wool and Mineral Fiber, multiply thickness in inches by 3.142857. For Cellulose, multiply inches by 3.6666 to find R-Value. Or better yet, use the"AUTO COMMENTS." Insulation usually comes in four Types: Loose-fill, Batts, Rolls and Rigid Foam Board. Fiberglass is recycled glass and sand, Rock Wool is recycled Steel scraps and Basaltic Rock, Cellulose is recycled newspapers treated with fire retardant chemicals. Rigid Foam Board (used on the exterior side of walls and behind the ceiling panel of a Cathedral ceiling) is obviously not visible or accessible during an inspection. A home can lose 50% of it's heat through the roof, with 25% going through the walls and windows, and 25% through the floor.

II-5D7E2FBB-08F3-480A-9315-F345621255AA.title: SUMP PUMP
II-5D7E2FBB-08F3-480A-9315-F345621255AA.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is the sump pump in a proper container?

2. Does the drain for the sump pump exit the building?

3. Is there a proper GFCI outlet provided?

4. The sump pump must not be using an extension cord or temporary wiring.

More Info:

  1. Sump pumps work fine when all the water is removed and air dries out the crawlspace within 2-3 days. If all the water is not removed, then the pump is not adequate and more corrective action is needed.
  2. When recommending a sump pump be installed, you should think about trenches around the perimeter with gravel installed leading to the lowest area and a way to exit water from building without using the sewer system, so our taxpayer dollars don't treat the rain water.
  3. Think about electricity which usually requires an electrical contractor to install a GFCI outlet within reach of the sump pump cord (no extension cords).
  4. Don't forget the plastic vapor barrier. If all that makes sense then it may solve a water problem. Another problem to look for is an approved sump pump container, not a bucket. What's the difference? A lot of difference, if a water infiltration expert comes behind you slinging mud. A bucket with a few drain holes in the bottom should work - but I would reference in my report that the bucket while appears to work fine is not an approved sump pump container as some repair specialist may note.
  5. Don't forget to raise the rod and float to see if it actually works.

II-5EFBF48D-F2C9-4466-8B73-32F1729A3FBD.title: ROOF FLASHINGS
II-5EFBF48D-F2C9-4466-8B73-32F1729A3FBD.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is there a lack of or improper flashing at wall junctions or chimneys?

2. Does dormer siding have sufficient clearance from the roof? Is it flashed properly?

More Info:

  1. Flashings are hidden most of the time, but you can go to the roof and wall junctions and tap on the shingle to see if it flexes away from the flashing underneath.
  2. Know what step flashing is, along with cap or counter flashing. The cap or counter flashing provides a hood over the step flashing and is bent and inserted into a masonry cut groove in brick or block. Flashing a rock chimney after a roof tear off is near impossible to do properly because you can't cut a groove in rock to tuck in bent flashing. The cap flashing is then laid flush and caulked at top, often failing in a short period of time.
  3. There is a product called Peel-n-Seal that is a foil backed sheet of tar and is pliable. It comes in a roll that can be cut with a knife and after peeling off wax paper can be molded to fit and seal against uneven surfaces like rock or stone. Some guys heat up the tar backing first with a butane torch for immediate sealing, depending on outside temperatures. This doesn't look as good as copper, but is a lot better than not installing proper cap or counter flashing.

II-613EA8A3-5B3F-4ADE-A615-9AC6C791E328.title: SEPTIC FIELD
II-613EA8A3-5B3F-4ADE-A615-9AC6C791E328.helpHtml: We do not inspect water filtration units. Recommend contacting the installer for information on life expectancy or condition.

II-628D84A1-A8B7-44A3-AEB2-4E5AB32C0DDC.title: DUCTS AND VENTS
II-628D84A1-A8B7-44A3-AEB2-4E5AB32C0DDC.helpHtml: Make sure you note if a room does not have a register or vent. Also inspect all ductwork accessible. Note if the ductwork is not insulated if there is AC. Many times the tape is failing and the ductpipe has pulled loose from register underneath floor.

II-6448E54A-12EE-445C-BF9E-31006DA64550.title: DISTRIBUTION SYSTEMS (including fans, pumps, ducts and piping, with supports, insulation, air filters, registers, radiators, fan coil units and convectors)
II-6448E54A-12EE-445C-BF9E-31006DA64550.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Inspect filter condition and look for a good seal around the filter door or compartment?

2. Is there damaged or loose ductwork, duct tape?

3. Does the furnace or airhandler shut off when the blower door is removed (safety switch)?

More Info:

  1. Make sure you note if a room does not have a register or vent.
  2. Also inspect all ductwork accessible. Note if the ductwork is not insulated if there is AC.
  3. Many times the tape is failing and the ductpipe has pulled loose from the register underneath the floor.
  4. Pull out or examine the filter as part of your air handler inspection. Many times the filter is the wrong size or clogged beyond belief.
  5. A clogged filter can cause $10 a month in electricity costs and shorten the life of the unit not to mention the poor air quality.
  6. New construction: Make sure you try to look deep inside the return air cavity in the wall to look for unhealthy items left behind by sub contractors.
  7. Radiators for old boilers can clog or not heat fully. Sometimes they can be blown clean by a boiler technician and sometimes they cannot. One radiator could cost $1000 or more easily ($80 a rung so I've heard) so be sure and write up any that do not get hot on both ends as needing servicing or further inspection by a Boiler technician.
  8. Read the auto-comments in the heat section.

Reference Materials:

II-64B8E991-697E-4ECF-8F6A-F595A77E89BC.title: INTERIOR WATER SUPPLY AND DISTRIBUTION SYSTEMS AND FIXTURES
II-64B8E991-697E-4ECF-8F6A-F595A77E89BC.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Did you tug on the hose bib(s) and test them for operation?

2. Did you write in the report that you did not remove garden hose to check for a drip?

3. Does the spray nozzle leak or drip above or below the sink when faucet is turned on? Is the aerator working?

4. Does the plumbing system pass the functional flow test? (Run a shower at bathing temperature and then turn on the sink faucets and flush the toilet. If you can still take a shower, it passes).

(Toilets)

5. Does the toilet tank lid fit properly?

6. Does the tank have condensation leaking onto the floor?

7. Is the toilet loose at the floor connection? Are there leak signs?

8. Was the vinyl floor cut around the toilet?

9. Did you check the floor on each side of toilet with your weight?

10. Lift the toilet tank lid and inspect water quality (iron or sediment). Some sellers will attempt to clean or hide iron problems before the inspection but they forget about cleaning inside the toilet tank

(Shower or bathtubs)

11. Are the tub faucets or shower arm loose in the wall when tugged on?

12. Are the hot and cold faucets reversed?

13. Are any bathtubs missing a shower?

14. Are there any corroded galvanized supply lines? Wet joints? Are they supported ok?

15. Old concrete sinks need to be partially filled to check for leaks.

16. Check for poly piping and use auto-comment if poly is present

17. Indicate whether or not the jet powered tub worked properly

More Info:

  1. Be sure to check in several areas throughout your inspection on the type of water supply or distribution materials in the home. Sometimes there are several in one home.
  2. Poly piping has become a concern. The real negative is that some people believe that it is not "if" but "when" the poly will fail. It is estimated that poly will fail within 15 years of installation. Whether this is true or not, it is important for you to know that someone may say that in court for the plaintiff and you might be the defendant. Keep that in mind.
  3. Pex material comes in colors and replaces poly as far as flexibility in installation.
  4. CPVC is easy to install but freeze breaks can split CPVCcausing significant damage. Instead of a small split in the pipe like will happen with copper, CPVC can take out many feet if not all the exposed piping that froze.
  5. Copper seems to be the tried and true choice.
  6. Toilet tanks can tell a lot. I have had sellers with iron problems clean all the brown from all fixtures before inspection and then lift the tank lid and see what they missed. Great time to take a picture.

II-64BF208E-7D50-4D07-B913-9DCFF1A1E904.title: COUNTERS AND A REPRESENTATIVE NUMBER OF CABINETS
II-64BF208E-7D50-4D07-B913-9DCFF1A1E904.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Check the countertop at sink rim for absorption or damage.

2. Check the backside of drawers at the cabinet base for mold.

3. Check the wall behind the refrigerator for mold.

4. Check the Icemaker line behind the refrigerator for kinks or damage.

5. Are there any extra large cut-outs for plumbing or the range vent that may allow air infiltration from the attic or crawlspace?

6. What is the microwave clearance from the range?

7. Is the sink base deteriorated or sagging from previous leaks at the bottom shelf?

8. Does the back splash on the counter behind the sink prevent splash water from possibly going behind sink base and causing mold on concealed wall?

9. Is the kick board missing anywhere in the kitchen cabinetry that may allow trash to collect or rodents to enter?

10. Is the wall cabinetry secure?

11. Is the shelving warped?

12. Make sure the island cabinet cannot be moved if a wired outlet is present

More Info:

  1. For new home construction, it is important to look for workmanship flaws in installation and mounting of cabinets or securing the countertop.
  2. Cabinets are expensive and you should be aware of high expectations from your client on having near perfect workmanship and installations of crown, trim, joining sides of two cabinets, cut-out for the dishwasher and cut-outs for the plumbing lines the size of a baseball.
  3. Islands that are moveable but have a wired outlet, should be noted as well.
  4. The dishwasher needs to be secured under the counter.
  5. Tile counters should not be sharp or have the cut edge exposed along the counter edge (sharp).
  6. Make sure counters that overhang or extend towards a range top are not to close to the rear burner or heating element because of a fire hazard.
  7. Remember, in new construction, there are no excuses for less than near perfect cabinet installation.

II-650B9614-1318-47C6-A1F3-8405728FE2B8.title: FOOD WASTE DISPOSER
II-650B9614-1318-47C6-A1F3-8405728FE2B8.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is the disposer wiring missing romex connectors?

2. Is there a loose wiring splice?

3. Is there any loose wiring under the sink where the disposer used to be?

4. If the power switch to the disposal is below a countertop, a child could inadvertently turn it on

More Info:

  1. Check wiring and the romex connector.
  2. Check the drain and sink mount.
  3. Use a flashlight to inspect blades for rust or obstruction. Note if the rubber strainer/shield is worn out.
  4. Run water and turn on disposer. Turn water off and listen to the disposer and note if it is noisy, obstructed etc.
  5. Rusted blades usually means dull blades or perhaps replacement.

II-66876BE9-83BA-4681-9A1F-E26F4BF4FA74.title: CEILING and FLOORS
II-66876BE9-83BA-4681-9A1F-E26F4BF4FA74.helpHtml: Look at an old home with an old eye. Always note water stains and whether or not you can determine how old they are by a moisture meter, examining the area related in attic and on roof. On newer homes, note nail pops, exposed or loose sheetrock tape and repair signs. Workmanship is important on all homes but especially new ones. Look for signs of only one coat of paint or poor sanding, nail indentations etc. Look at perimeter of floor for water stains or deterioration. Bounce around a little on the floor (without lifting your feet). Note any areas damaged on floor covering, including stains, exposed seams, small tears or blemishes etc. See Discoveries and Comments

II-683FFD99-F3FC-4C8E-B706-27C419D4FFC3.title: GARAGE DOOR OPERATORS (Report whether or not doors will reverse when met with resistance)
II-683FFD99-F3FC-4C8E-B706-27C419D4FFC3.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is the auto-opener using a light fixture adapter or an extension cord that's not approved?

2. Look for a missing cover, burnt cover, missing bulb etc.

3. Look for the electrical plug and make sure it has a proper outlet in reach.

4. Some doors do not reverse when met with resistance and could kill. Always be concerned about that.

5. The reason why the door needs to reverse when met with resistance, even with sensors in place, is because if a truck bed or bumper was extended into the door path and is higher than the sensors, major damage would occur.

6. Doors that need adjustment in order to reverse may not be able to be adjusted. Sometimes the adjustment screws/knobs will not adjust it properly.

7. Check for height to accommodate most vehicles or let them know a large car may not fit.

More Info:

Quick Check:

More Info:

  1. They make a cool microwave tester. You can get them in any inspector tool mag.
  2. Be alert that in older homes, they may have added a microwave to the kitchen's existing circuitry and may be on a shared circuit. Sometimes an older microwave worked fine but a new one can draw more amps and trip the circuit. Microwaves should have their own 20 amp dedicated circuit but in many older homes, they do not.

II-70B3A86D-60ED-483D-9909-A8045A4C06A8.title: ROOF COVERINGS
II-70B3A86D-60ED-483D-9909-A8045A4C06A8.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Are there any noticeable sways or sags in the roof?

2. Do you estimate the life remaining on the roof covering to be 5 years or less?

3. Are there any repair signs on the roof?

4. Are there any sides or areas of the roof that were not inspected due to noaccess?

More Info:

  1. I don't get up on all roofs, but many if not most of the roofs I see are accessible. These are walkable roofs and not too steep.
  2. Hair-line cracks that sometimes occur on shingles cannot be seen unless you go up on the roof. Caulking or repair signs can be missed as well. If you're on the roof, look for boot flange for vent pipes to see if they fit the pipe to keep out rain.
  3. I don't walk on tile roofs or wood shakes for fear of damaging them or falling.
  4. Never step out on a metal awning.

The home inspector is not required to: Walk on the roofing; or Observe attached accessories including but not limited to solar systems, antennae, and lightning arrestors.

II-72833760-0FEA-414B-9BF7-EBB5D6C1B35A.helpHtml: Most everyone expects electric 220-volt connection for Dryer. Note if the only connection for dryer is gas. Note if both are available as a plus. Make sure the waste line for plumbing has a trap and vent. Many older homes still have 1"1/2 diameter wasteline and new washing machines have stronger pumps that may over run drain. Not all but some. Look for signs on wall or floor, or the drain hose may have been modified in some way."Gray water" is a term that means that the water drains into the yard and not the sewer or septic. This could be a violation in your area. Consult with the health dept or building safety on this issue. Some septic tanks were not designed for the volume of washing machine and could clog if gray water was connected to it. If you discover gray water use, note the possibilities. The outlet for washing machine should be grounded if existing. A repair would be a GFCI outlet.

2. Did you write in the report that you did not remove garden hose to check for a drip?

3. Does the spray nozzle leak or drip above or below the sink when faucet is turned on? Is the aerator working?

4. Does the plumbing system pass the functional flow test? (Run a shower at bathing temperature and then turn on the sink faucets and flush the toilet. If you can still take a shower, it passes).

(Toilets)

5. Does the toilet tank lid fit properly?

6. Does the tank have condensation leaking onto the floor?

7. Is the toilet loose at the floor connection? Are there leak signs?

8. Was the vinyl floor cut around the toilet?

9. Did you check the floor on each side of toilet with your weight?

10. Lift the toilet tank lid and inspect water quality (iron or sediment). Some sellers will attempt to clean or hide iron problems before the inspection but they forget about cleaning inside the toilet tank

(Shower or bathtubs)

11. Are the tub faucets or shower arm loose in the wall when tugged on?

12. Are the hot and cold faucets reversed?

13. Are any bathtubs missing a shower?

14. Are there any corroded galvanized supply lines? Wet joints? Are they supported ok?

15. Old concrete sinks need to be partially filled to check for leaks.

16. Check for poly piping and use auto-comment if poly is present

17. Indicate whether or not the jet powered tub worked properly

  2. One must also consider: Why isn't one there? It could be the size of the heat/AC unit which would require a bigger unit or perhaps there is no physical way to install one. Extreme remodeling may be involved.
  3. Also, stay alert for the type of heating system in the house with an AC condenser. If it's boiler heat and there is an AC unit outside, and the house is 2 story, it is likely that the AC serves the upstairs only. Therefore it is necessary to point this out in your report.

II-74D8F45F-9F8A-44B9-9B47-945BB55544BB.title: HOT WATER SYSTEMS, CONTROLS, CHIMNEYS, FLUES AND VENTS
II-74D8F45F-9F8A-44B9-9B47-945BB55544BB.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is the gas water heater 18" off the floor and mounted on a proper stand or support?

2. Is the water heater strapped securely to the wall (required in earthquake zones)?

3. If the gas line to the water heater or furnace could be bumped or ruptured by a vehicle, a pole or guard post should be recommended

4. If the water heater is in the crawlspace or basement, it should not be lower than ground level. You may not dig a hole to set the water heater in.

5. Use a lighter at the draft hood when the gas water heater is on to check for proper draw.

6. A gas water heater in the closet needs fresh air from the attic at the ceiling and near the floor.

More Info:

  1. Inspect the plumbing connections and tank housing.
  2. Note rust signs from moisture or condensation (if in a damp area of building) or possible leak at the liner.
  3. Rust along the bottom can be caused when water leaks out while changing heating elements. Sometimes it's hard to distinguish. If you discover rust along the bottom, then remove panel access and feel the insulation to determine if it's currently wet.
  4. Water heaters installed in a crawlspace should not be below ground level.
  5. Gas water heaters installed in a garage should be at least 18 inches off the ground.
  6. When two gas vent pipes enter the chimney together, the highest BTU should enter chimney under the smaller BTU.
  7. Gas water heaters should have the thermostat turned up to force it to come on in order to test the draw at the diverter with a match or lighter. If the draw does not noticeably suck in flame on a match, there could be a venting problem.
  8. White deposits and rust on metal vent pipe can occur from moisture in the gas when not venting properly.
  9. A greasy residue on top of the gas water heater is also a sign of a vent problem.
  10. A blackened or smoky appearance on and around the housing near the flame of a gas water heater indicates the need for more air (combustion air).
  11. The T&P valve (Test and Pressure or Pop off valve) can look fine if the building has not had the water heater on 24 hours before inspection. It can then leak after the buyer moves in. The primary reason is that pressure on the system builds up at night when no one is using water. With gas, the added pressure is a result of steam. Be aware of this when you inspect a vacant building and the water heater has not been on for 24 hours prior.

3. Are bushes or a fence obstructing air flow?

5. Are there any electric outlets located on the wall above the electric baseboard which could be a possible fire hazard?

  14. Check for back drafting by using a lighter or match around joints in the vent pipe, or at an existing test hole (if any).
  15. Steam boilers have a sight glass to check water level.
  16. Circulating boilers do not have a sight glass.
  17. Boilers should be flushed regularly as part of a normal maintenance schedule.
  18. ( HEAT PUMPS ) should not be ran in AC mode if temp outside is @ 65 degrees or less. You could damage the unit.
  19. Be sure and note if you did not inspect it. Just because you have heat coming out of the registers doesn't mean your compressor outside is working.
  20. The fan outside should be moving. Just because the fan outside is moving doesn't mean you have heat.

  24. Only trouble shooting by a qualified heat contractor can determine exactly.
  25. The ambient air test differential on a heat pump should be between 14 and 22 degrees. Use a thermometer at the main plenum and use one at the return air at the air handler. The difference in these (in AC mode) should be 14 to 22 degrees.

The home inspector shall observe permanently installed heating systems including: Heating equipment; Normal operating controls; Automatic safety controls; Chimneys, flues, and vents, where readily visible; Solid fuel heating devices; Heat distribution systems including fans, pumps, ducts and piping, with supports, insulation, air filters, registers, radiators, fan coil units, convectors; and the presence of an installed heat source in each room. II-7A654DFA-D8D1-4133-872C-5CADFA7B080C.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Are there bushes against the siding?

2. Is the siding in contact with the ground or mulch?

3. Check the siding at planter boxes, stacked wood and downspout locations.

4. Is siding deteriorated where the the deck attaches to home (above deck)?

5. Are there any lifted nails, discolored or loose siding?

6. Are there any repairs to siding or soffits that is inconsistent?

7. Is there any staining or discoloration that warrants a finger pressure test on soffits, fascia, column bases, window sills, porch flooring or bottom of door jambs?

8. Do you see where the dryer vent terminates outside?

More Info:

Circle the house slowly, paying special attention behind shrubs or hard to reach areas. Check for loose or lifted nails, deterioration, paint peel, caulking at seams, joints, trim, along the top of garage door and window brick mold.

  1. Swelling of composite siding with recessed nails, green algae areas
    should be noted.
  2. Ground clearance of six inches or better where possible is recommended.
  3. Problem areas to look for are where roof stops at chimney wall (roof junction) or where the end of the gutter butts against another wall of the home.
  4. Look for siding in contact with ground.
  5. Look under windows, at dormers and above deck at starter row.

Reference Materials:

The home inspector shall observe: Wall cladding, flashings, and trim; Entryway doors and a representative number of windows; Garage door operators; Decks, balconies, stoops, steps, areaways, porches and applicable railings; Eaves, soffits, and fascias; and Vegetation, grading, drainage, driveways, patios, walkways, and retaining walls with respect to their effect on the condition of the building. The home inspector shall: Describe wall cladding materials; Operate all entryway doors and a representative number of windows; Operate garage doors manually or by using permanently installed controls for any garage door operator; Report whether or not any garage door operator will automatically reverse or stop when meeting reasonable resistance during closing; and Probe exterior wood components where deterioration is suspected.

The home inspector is not required to observe: Storm windows, storm doors, screening, shutters, awnings, and similar seasonal accessories; Fences; Presence of safety glazing in doors and windows;Garage door operator remote control transmitters; Geological conditions; Soil conditions; Recreational facilities (including spas, saunas, steam baths, swimming pools, tennis courts, playground equipment, and other exercise, entertainment, or athletic facilities); Detached buildings or structures; or Presence or condition of buried fuel storage tanks.

II-7B75517F-5217-4031-85D0-A286CFDC95DD.title: FLOORS (Structural)
II-7B75517F-5217-4031-85D0-A286CFDC95DD.helpHtml: Look at an old home with an old eye. Always note water stains and whether or not you can determine how old they are by a moisture meter, examining the area related in attic and on roof. Newer homes note nail pops, exposed or loose sheetrock tape and repair signs. Workmanship is important on all homes but especially new ones. Look for signs of only one coat of paint or poor sanding, nail indentations etc. Look at perimeter of floor for water stains or deterioration. Bounce around a little on the floor (without lifting your feet). Note any areas damaged on floor covering, including stains, exposed seams, small tear or blemish etc. See Discoveries and Comments

II-7CB18662-E615-46FC-85B8-B893904D30B5.title: FUEL STORAGE AND DISTRIBUTION SYSTEMS (Interior fuel storage, piping, venting, supports, leaks)
II-7CB18662-E615-46FC-85B8-B893904D30B5.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is the oil barrel or propane tank leaning, leaking, or too small for the building?

2. Is the oil barrel stand leaning or weak? Are there stains on the ground from oil drips?

3. Are the oil or gas fuel lines damaged or kinked?

4. Does the Gas Dryer have a shut-off valve above the floor?

5. The Natural Gas lineshould not be soft copper until it comes through the floor or walls

More Info:

  1. Always tell the client when you discover an oil barrel in the ground.
  2. Always tell them that you did not test the soil for possible contamination or if the oil barrel is leaking or not.
  3. Always make sure that gas piping has a cap on any unused end.
  4. Soft copper piping for gas is not allowed in my area unless it is propane. This is when the piping travels through floors or walls etc. and can only change to soft piping like copper above the floor. A shut-off valve above the floor is required.

II-8352D735-390B-4882-891A-96E3EA1EB2C0.title: EAVES, SOFFITS AND FASCIAS
II-8352D735-390B-4882-891A-96E3EA1EB2C0.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

2. Are there any repairs to siding or soffits that is inconsistent?

3. Is there any staining or discoloration that warrants a finger pressure test on soffits, fascia, column bases, window sills, porch flooring or bottom of door jambs?

4. Do you notice any new paint peel or bubbling that indicates a leak has not been corrected at eaves or fascias?

5. If it's raining during the inspection, it may be difficult to detect deterioration of the eaves and roof and you may need to note a "not inspected" for these areas.

More Info:

  1. Look for paint bubbles or wrinkles in paint, then poke and check them. Eaves or soffit panels can hide soft deterioration until poked or touched.
  2. Clogged gutters in the past may have rotted soffits or eaves.
  3. When dealing with exposed eaves, look for the starter or first run of roof board for deterioration.
  4. Dark painted wood on the second story can hide deterioration well. If its raining during your inspection and you have a second story eave painted dark it will be very difficult to spot deterioration (been there - done that). Check to see if vents are applicable or needed and intact.
