The home inspector shall: Move insulation where readily visible evidence indicates the need to do so; and Move insulation where chimneys penetrate roofs, where plumbing drain/waste pipes penetrate floors, adjacent to earth filled stoops or porches, and at exterior doors.

The home inspector is not required to report on: Concealed insulation and vapor retarders; or Venting equipment that is integral with household appliances.

II-DCD21CBA-6DF7-4D91-8FEA-7DB4B090C36E.title: RANGE HOOD
II-DCD21CBA-6DF7-4D91-8FEA-7DB4B090C36E.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

More Info:
Turn on the exhaust fan, observe if a filter is in place and inspect vent pipe. Check the light and fan speeds. Check any visible wiring or outlets.

II-DF6F23AF-A268-4D91-9359-785D13B7E2D9.title: HEATING EQUIPMENT
II-DF6F23AF-A268-4D91-9359-785D13B7E2D9.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is the heat pump / condenser level?

2. Are the foam sleeves on the suction line intact?

3. Are bushes or a fence obstructing air flow?

4. Hydronic systems should have a water heater that is designed for heating the home and not use converted water heaters. Converted water heaters may not have a high enough BTU rating.

5. Are there any electric outlets located on the wall above the electric baseboard which could be a possible fire hazard?

More Info:

  1. Heating Equipment over 15 years old and still operating should still be noted as old, and recommend servicing them annually to monitor for safe operation.
  2. (Oil furnaces) Check around the sight hole for smoke stains around the collar that may be leaking fumes.
  3. Examine the vent pipe and where it enters chimney for integrity and proper seal.
  4. Check for back drafting by using a lighter or match around joints in the vent pipe, or at an existing test hole (if any).
  5. An erratic movement of the damper lid on the vent pipe and/or soot build-up should be noted.
  6. The furnace should run for at least 15 minutes.
  7. It's a good technique to observe the firing, or ignition, of the furnace. To do this, use the cut-off switch at the furnace before you set the thermostat to turn the furnace on. If it's not running normally, recommend a licensed heat contractor for service and repair as needed.
  8. Learn how to perform a smoke bomb test. Use a Gas Tracer.
  9. ( GAS FURNACES ) Use a gas tracer around the unit. Examine burners and raceway for charred bits and recommend service if bits are excessive or flame is not even.
  10. If flame dances sharply or rolls under the burner recommend service.
  11. Heat exchangers or the steel liner is more likely to crack near the pilot light.
  12. ( BOILERS ) should be tested for 30 to 45 minutes to allow all radiators to heat fully. Some radiators that are old may take longer to heat but you have to decide while your there if they heat from one end to the other. This time is needed to allow pressure to build and check for leaks. Radiators are extremely expensive and you don't want to miss even one. If over 15 years old and operating well it should be noted as old and recommend servicing annually to monitor for safe operation.
  13. Check around the sight hole for smoke stains around the collar that may be leaking fumes. Examine the vent pipe and where it enters the chimney for integrity and proper seal.
  14. Check for back drafting by using a lighter or match around joints in the vent pipe, or at an existing test hole (if any).
  15. Steam boilers have a sight glass to check water level.
  16. Circulating boilers do not have a sight glass.
  17. Boilers should be flushed regularly as part of a normal maintenance schedule.
  18. ( HEAT PUMPS ) should not be ran in AC mode if temp outside is @ 65 degrees or less. You could damage the unit.
  19. Be sure and note if you did not inspect it. Just because you have heat coming out of the registers doesn't mean your compressor outside is working.
  20. The fan outside should be moving. Just because the fan outside is moving doesn't mean you have heat.
  21. Grab the suction line before it enters air handler inside and feel for heat.
  22. In summer, hand check the suction line for ice cold. No cold feeling means recommending service.
  23. The coils inside the air handler may need cleaning or the liquid line may need refrigerant.
  24. Only trouble shooting by a qualified heat contractor can determine exactly.
  25. The ambient air test differential on a heat pump should be between 14 and 22 degrees. Use a thermometer at the main plenum and use one at the return air at the air handler. The difference in these (in AC mode) should be 14 to 22 degrees.
  26. ( ELECTRIC BASE ) should be turned on and checked for proper operation, securely fastened to wall or floor.
  27. There should never be an outlet on the wall directly above electric base.
  28. Remove the front cover on the baseboard and inspect the wire that runs the length of the base located inside a tube. This wire can become brittle or weak over time, and cause abnormal heating up of unit and can cause a fire.

Reference Materials:

The home inspector shall observe permanently installed heating systems including: Heating equipment; Normal operating controls; Automatic safety controls; Chimneys, flues, and vents, where readily visible; Solid fuel heating devices; Heat distribution systems including fans, pumps, ducts and piping, with supports, insulation, air filters, registers, radiators, fan coil units, convectors; and the presence of an installed heat source in each room. The home inspector shall describe: Energy source; and Heating equipment and distribution type. The home inspector shall operate the systems using normal operating controls. The home inspector shall open readily openable access panels provided by the manufacturer or installer for routine homeowner maintenance.

The home inspector is not required to: Operate heating systems when weather conditions or other circumstances may cause equipment damage; Operate automatic safety controls; Ignite or extinguish solid fuel fires; or Observe: The interior of flues; Fireplace insert flue connections; Humidifiers; Electronic air filters; or The uniformity or adequacy of heat supply to the various rooms.

II-E0D01FB1-4C6C-43CC-BE2F-6691A55CFF26.title: POLARITY AND GROUNDING OF RECEPTACLES WITHIN 6 FEET OF INTERIOR PLUMBING FIXTURES, AND ALL RECEPTACLES IN GARAGE, CARPORT,  EXTERIOR WALLS OF INSPECTED STRUCTURE
II-E0D01FB1-4C6C-43CC-BE2F-6691A55CFF26.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Do you notice any GFCI outlets with freezers plugged into them? Don't forget to reset GFCI. Two prong plugs in the Garage or around any areas with water?

More Info:

  1. I use a simple three-prong plug with a GFCI test button. It identifies whether or not the outlet is grounded, and if the polarity is correct.
  2. Some tips are: Your three-prong GFCI test plug will not "trip" the outlet if it is a non-grounded GFCI. But it still should trip by pressing the test button on outlet, and kill the circuit.
  3. A non-grounded outlet can be corrected by either attaching a ground wire to the outlet and attach it to a metal rod or a metal plumbing pipe.
  4. Or, replace the three-prongnon-grounded outlet with a three-prong GFCI outlet. A sticker should be on the outlet that identifies it as non-grounded.
  5. Or last, change the circuit breaker to a GFCI breaker at the panel.
  6. You can "trip" a non-grounded GFCI with a voltmeter by placing one prong of the voltmeter in the short slit of the outlet, and take the other prong of the voltmeter and touch a metal plumbing pipe (that eventually contacts the soil).
  7. Most three-prong GFCI plugs will show two lights at the end of the plug when the outlet being tested is grounded. When you press the button on the plug, both lights should remain lit and strong. If however, the plug lights up only one of the two grounding lights "Faint or Dim" and you press the button on the plug and it shows "Reverse polarity", it may just be a "loose" ground wire and can be corrected a lot easier than having to install a new ground wire.
  8. Just because you can press the test button on the GFCI outlet using your finger and it "trips," doesn't mean it killed the circuit. It could be defective.
  9. New GFCI outlets can be defective when installed.
  10. Always use the three-prong GFCI test plug on every three-prong outlet.
  11. Homeowners frequently use a freezer in their garage. Most outlets in the garage are on a GFCI Circuit. When you're inspecting the home don't forget to reset the GFCI outlet or you may be buying the homeowners spoiled food.

Reference Materials:

II-E1BBFF84-F172-484C-97E4-3B06B7958340.title: WALL CLADDING FLASHING  AND TRIM
II-E1BBFF84-F172-484C-97E4-3B06B7958340.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Are there bushes against the siding?

2. Is the siding in contact with the ground or mulch?

3. Check the siding at planter boxes, stacked wood and downspout locations.

4. Is siding deteriorated where the the deck attaches to home (above deck)?

5. Are there any lifted nails, discolored or loose siding?

6. Are there any repairs to siding or soffits that is inconsistent?

7. Is there any staining or discoloration that warrants a finger pressure test on soffits, fascia, column bases, window sills, porch flooring or bottom of door jambs?

8. Do you see where the dryer vent terminates outside?

More Info:

Circle the house slowly, paying special attention behind shrubs or hard to reach areas. Check for loose or lifted nails, deterioration, paint peel, caulking at seams, joints, trim, along the top of garage door and window brick mold.

  1. Swelling of composite siding with recessed nails, green algae areas
    should be noted.
  2. Ground clearance of six inches or better where possible is recommended.
  3. Problem areas to look for are where roof stops at chimney wall (roof junction) or where the end of the gutter butts against another wall of the home.
  4. Look for siding in contact with ground.
  5. Look under windows, at dormers and above deck at starter row.

Reference Materials:

The home inspector shall observe: Wall cladding, flashings, and trim; Entryway doors and a representative number of windows; Garage door operators; Decks, balconies, stoops, steps, areaways, porches and applicable railings; Eaves, soffits, and fascias; and Vegetation, grading, drainage, driveways, patios, walkways, and retaining walls with respect to their effect on the condition of the building. The home inspector shall: Describe wall cladding materials; Operate all entryway doors and a representative number of windows; Operate garage doors manually or by using permanently installed controls for any garage door operator; Report whether or not any garage door operator will automatically reverse or stop when meeting reasonable resistance during closing; and Probe exterior wood components where deterioration is suspected.

The home inspector is not required to observe: Storm windows, storm doors, screening, shutters, awnings, and similar seasonal accessories; Fences; Presence of safety glazing in doors and windows;Garage door operator remote control transmitters; Geological conditions; Soil conditions; Recreational facilities (including spas, saunas, steam baths, swimming pools, tennis courts, playground equipment, and other exercise, entertainment, or athletic facilities); Detached buildings or structures; or Presence or condition of buried fuel storage tanks.

II-E9B6CBF2-E94D-4419-8E69-1C8E8EA33B0E.title: ROOF COVERINGS
II-E9B6CBF2-E94D-4419-8E69-1C8E8EA33B0E.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Are there any noticeable sways or sags in the roof?

2. Do you estimate the life remaining on the roof covering to be 4 years or less?

3. Are there any repair signs on the roof?

4. Are there any sides or areas of the roof that were not inspected due to no access?

More Info:

  1. I don't get up on all roofs, but many if not most of the roofs I see are accessible. These are walkable roofs and not too steep.
  2. Hair-line cracks that sometimes occur on shingles cannot be seen unless you go up on the roof. Caulking or repair signs can be missed as well. If you're on the roof, look for boot flange for vent pipes to see if they fit the pipe to keep out rain.
  3. I don't walk on tile roofs or wood shakes for fear of damaging them or falling.
  4. Never step out on a metal awning.

The home inspector shall observe: Roof covering; Roof drainage systems; Flashings; Skylights, chimneys, and roof penetrations; and signs of' leaks or abnormal condensation on building components. The home inspector shall: Describe the type of roof covering materials; and Report the methods used to observe the roofing.

The home inspector is not required to: Walk on the roofing; or Observe attached accessories including but not limited to solar systems, antennae, and lightning arrestors.

II-EA42EB57-03DF-4601-BA47-648B621C0E0C.helpHtml: Be sure and comment on any negative slope towards home that may cause problems like erosion, water intrusion and silt travel. The home inspector shall observe: Central air conditioning systems including: Cooling and air handling equipment; and Normal operating controls. Distribution systems including: Fans, pumps, ducts and piping, with associated supports, dampers, insulation, air filters, registers, fan-coil units; and The presence of an installed cooling source in each room. The home inspector shall describe: Energy sources; and Cooling equipment type. The home inspector shall operate the systems using normal operating controls. The home inspector shall open readily openable access panels provided by the manufacturer or installer for routine homeowner maintenance

The home inspector is not required to:Operate cooling systems when weather conditions or other circumstances may cause equipment damage; Observe non-central air conditioners; or Observe the uniformity or adequacy of cool-air supply to the various rooms. Ambient air test is when you stick two meat thermometers into the main plenum of the air handler. One in the return air and one in the supply. Preferably near each other at the main trunk. If the AC has been running for an adequate amount of time before test you should see a range somewhere between 14 and 22 degrees. The supply should be the colder of the two. This test is not conclusive because of varying conditions but if it's out of range and the AC has had time to cool the home, then you can recommend an HVAC person (Heating Ventilation and Air Conditioning)

II-ECD6DEC2-E69B-46D3-A030-610062D72576.title: ELECTRICAL CONNECTED DEVICES AND FIXTURES
II-ECD6DEC2-E69B-46D3-A030-610062D72576.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is the refrigerator outlet 3 prong plug grounded?

(Baths)
2. Is there a duplex grounded outlet? If not recommend a GFCI when electrical contractor corrects.

3. The light fixture outlet in the bath should be disabled if not grounded.

4. There should be at least two outlets in each room.

5. Note any ceiling fans that wobble more than expected

6. Are there any electric outlets located on the wall above the electric baseboard, which is a possible fire hazard?

More Info:

  1. The inspection item CONNECTED DEVICES AND FIXTURES is for miscellaneous electrical items found around the property. (i.e. loose splices, boxes missing cover plates etc).
  2. I use a simple three-prong plug with a GFCI test button. It identifies whether or not the outlet is grounded, and if the polarity is correct.
  3. Some tips are: Your three-prong GFCI test plug will not "trip" the outlet if it is a non-grounded GFCI. It should still trip by pressing the test button on the outlet, and kill the circuit.
  4. A non-grounded outlet can be corrected by either attaching a ground wire to the outlet and attach it to a metal rod or a metal plumbing pipe.
  5. Or, replace the three-prongnon-grounded outlet with a three-prong GFCI outlet. A sticker should be on the outlet that identifies it as non-grounded.
  6. Or last, change the circuit breaker to a GFCI breaker at panel.
  7. You can "trip" a non-grounded GFCI with a voltmeter by placing one prong of the voltmeter in the short slit of the outlet, and take the other prong of the voltmeter and touch a metal plumbing pipe (that eventually contacts the soil).
  8. Most three-prong GFCI plugs will show two lights at the end of the plug when the outlet being tested is grounded. When you press the button on the plug, both lights should remain lit and strong. If however, the plug lights up only one of the two grounding lights "Faint or Dim" and you press the button on the plug and it shows "Reverse polarity", it may just be a "loose" ground wire and can be corrected a lot easier than having to install a new ground wire.
  9. Just because you can press the test button on the GFCI outlet using your finger and it "trips," doesn't mean it killed the circuit. It could be defective.
  10. New GFCI outlets that are installed can be defective.
  11. Always use the three-prong GFCI test plug on every three-prong outlet.
  12. Homeowners frequently use a freezer in their garage. Most outlets in the garage are on a GFCI Circuit. When you're inspecting the home, don't forget to reset the GFCI outlet or you may be buying the homeowners spoiled food.

II-EF139821-E0AF-4E84-9217-CC9ADFFC52AD.title: DOORS (Exterior)
II-EF139821-E0AF-4E84-9217-CC9ADFFC52AD.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is there any staining or discoloration that warrants a finger pressure test on exterior door trim /jambs at bottom (including sliding glass doors, patio doors, side lights etc.)?

2. Note if the main entry doors are hollow core which is not as secure as a solid core.

3. Does the garage door opening height and width seem normal?

4. The garage door must reverse when met with resistance regardless of whether or not they have sensors. Sensors should be no higher off the floor than 6" or according to manufacturer specs.

5. What is the condition of the weather-stripping at garage door floor and sides?

6. Check both sides of Garage door for damage?

7. The "jerk and let go" test for the garage door works best but there is a risk of damaging the door if you don't let go quick enough. A 2 x 4 block placed on floor can damage a metal door if door does not reverse (not recommended).

8. Note older garage door springs that do not have retention cables to contain the spring if the cable breaks.

More Info:

  1. Always open and shut a door from both sides and note whether or not the door latches.
  2. Also note if the door is out of square enough that it no longer ensures privacy.
  3. Check for holes in doors and for a doorstop on each one. Note any trim or hardware missing (check all doors).
  4. Basement or Crawlspace: Make sure that the door fits properly and is properly painted. Look at the ground in front of the door for negative slope that may allow water intrusion.
  5. Check to see if the door is delaminating or deteriorated at the bottom .
  6. Sliding glass and patio doors: Open and close doors as needed and check for "daylight" and continuous weather-stripping.
  7. Also, close the door with knob until it latches. Then turn deadbolt and check strike for proper alignment and a tight fit.
  8. Also look carefully at the glass, and check for "Cloudy" appearance or cracked glass. This is a good time to inspect the floor area around door for possible water intrusion or deterioration.
  9. Garage doors: Raise the garage door and lay a 2 x 4 block on the floor at the middle of the door opening (except a metal door that could be damaged by a 2 x 4 block). Document if the door reverses or not.
  10. If you use your hand to provide resistance and the door does not reverse, you can severely damage the door if you're not careful. The door can "fold-up" damaging the door panel and chain drive.
  11. Even if the door has electronic sensors, it still should reverse when met with resistance. Adjustment screws are usually found on the side and rear of opener. These door adjustment screws can be tricky to adjust.

Reference Materials:

II-F1612465-8F52-4BF8-B5EF-3CB78EE606C1.title: DOORS (Interior)
II-F1612465-8F52-4BF8-B5EF-3CB78EE606C1.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Found mostly in bathrooms...Does the door open against a wall mounted heater that can cause a fire hazard?

2. Are doorstops or hingestops present?

3. Do doors close and latch properly?

4. Check the closet bi-fold door hardware and note whether or not the doors operate properly

More Info:

  1. All doors should latch when closed and note if the jamb rubs, because seasonal change may make the door swell and have difficulty closing.
  2. Note missing hardware, doorstop, damage etc.
  3. Check bi-folds at the top hardware location for damage.
  4. It is common for bi-folds to need adjustment. Failing to note this can sometimes create a phone call from the buyer, complaining about the bi-fold doors. Sometimes the opening for a bi-fold door needs adjustment which could be significant cosmetic work to correct the opening.

II-F3761524-2354-4F77-AFC1-8E86BA7AFD0C.title: SERVICE AND GROUNDING EQUIPMENT,  MAIN OVERCURRENT DEVICE, MAIN AND DISTRIBUTION PANELS
II-F3761524-2354-4F77-AFC1-8E86BA7AFD0C.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is the meterbase secure on the wall?

2. Is a drip loop present at weather head?

3. Is the wall anchor in place?

4. Is there a bond wire that connects to the metal plumbing supply lines where supply enters building?

5. Is the Electrical panel missing screws?

6. Do the circuit breaker brands match the panel brand?

7. If the Meterbase is not upgraded but the electrical panel is... Ok, unless the service wire from the meterbase to the panel is upgraded, then the meterbase should have been upgraded also.

8. Is the Meterbase grounded with wire, secure clamp and ground rod?

9. The Main disconnect breaker should be on the outside panel if the inside panel is further than 5 feet from the meterbase.

10. Are there any rusted screws or bus connectors in any panels?

11. Are there any Knockout covers (blanks) missing?

12. Are there any wiring missing romex connectors where wire enters into the panel?

13. Are there any exposed wiring splices outside of the panel or on water heater?

14. Is the panel secure to the wall? Is the Meterbase secure to the wall?

15. Are any panels located too close to water? Hidden inside a cabinet? Not accessible?

More Info:

  1. A bond wire is a ground wire that grounds the panel to the metal plumbing that goes into the soil. A ground wire is the wire outside that goes from the meterbase to the ground rod. In some rural areas or abroad, a bond wire to the metal plumbing is acceptable as the only ground with no ground wire outside. This is on some older homes but not new construction. The problem occurs when the plumber removes the old galvanized metal plumbing and replaces it with plastic or PVC, which removes the only bond/ground wire. We can't depend on the plumber to make sure the electric panel is grounded.
  2. Some electrical contractors say that on some old glass globe meter bases that there is nowhere to put a ground. I have heard some electrical contractors disagree and say that there is always a way to ground the meterbase. So sometimes I write in the report when I see this situation that "there is only one ground wire found on the panel and it leads to a metal plumbing pipe that has been changed to non-metal and there is no ground". Or that it goes to a an older galvanized line that may get changed in the future by a plumber and disconnect the only ground for the panel. I recommend an electrical contractor add another ground wire.
  3. Circuit breaker brand should match the panel. An electrical contractor may point this out to your buyer after they purchase the building. I never used to care about mixed brands as long as they fit properly. But clearly on the label, each panel brand requires their circuit brand only or it will void the UL listing. This was enough to scare my buyer, and I decided that I would not buy any more breakers. Since then, I've discovered that some electrical contractors feel that some brands can mix because of companies merging. I disagree unless those names are also on that particular panel label. SIEMENS, ITE and GOULD supposedly are one company. MURRAY may also be a part of SIEMENS.
  4. WESTINGHOUSE, BRYANT AND CUTLER-HAMMER are supposedly one company.
  5. Remember: The electrical panel has a label on it. And somewhere it usually states that only their brand is allowed to be used. All other brands will void warranty or may be a hazard.
  6. General Switch Brand panel may allow other brands that will fit. If they do, they will indicate it on the label.
  7. When in doubt, recommend an electrical contractor. If a fire was to occur and later it was found that the source was from the panel and it had different breakers, the homeowner would not be denied the insurance claim. But, the insurance company may feel that the recent inspection should have revealed it. Especially when a UL label on the panel states that no other brand is allowed.
  8. The insurance company may seek compensation from the inspector in the form of litigation. Whether they do or don't, right is right and wrong is wrong, so I mention it.
  9. There should also be a ground wire attached to a driven ground rod at the meter base. This grounds the panel itself.
  10. Some local electrical contractors may say that one is really good enough (at plumbing or meter base). But that's true only if the supply lines are not metal (Pex, CPVC etc.). If only the metal plumbing has a ground and not the meter base, and the metal plumbing is old corroded galvanized piping that gets replaced with Pex, there would then be no ground.
  11. Or, if the plumber replaced the old piping with copper or metal, it would be up to him to reset the ground and clamp onto the new pipe. And we all know plumbers aren't electrical contractors.

II-F565F7C0-684F-4DE7-A6C4-9B2C599EB32E.title: CEILINGS
II-F565F7C0-684F-4DE7-A6C4-9B2C599EB32E.helpHtml: Look at an old home with an old eye. Always note water stains and whether or not you can determine how old they are by a moisture meter, examining the area related in attic and on roof. Newer homes note nail pops, exposed or loose sheetrock tape and repair signs. Workmanship is important on all homes but especially new ones. Look for signs of only one coat of paint or poor sanding, nail indentations etc. Look at perimeter of floor for water stains or deterioration. Bounce around a little on the floor (without lifting your feet). Note any areas damaged on floor covering, including stains, exposed seams, small tear or blemish etc. See Discoveries and Comments

II-F7D63133-2E9F-46EB-9037-3A64302D8B8D.title: DISTRIBUTION SYSTEMS (including fans, pumps, ducts and piping, with supports, insulation, air filters, registers, radiators, fan coil units and convectors)
II-F7D63133-2E9F-46EB-9037-3A64302D8B8D.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Inspect the filter condition and look for a poor seal around the filter door or compartment.

2. Is there damaged or loose ductwork, duct tape?

3. Does the furnace or airhandler shut off when the blower door is removed (safety switch)?

4. Note any possible asbestos on old boilers, radiator piping or vent pipe to chimney (older homes). Sometimes asbestos can be found on the underside of decorative radiator covers inside home.

More Info:

  1. Make sure you note if a room does not have a register or vent.
  2. Also inspect all ductwork accessible.
  3. Note if the ductwork is not insulated, if there is AC.
  4. Many times the tape is failing and the ductpipe has pulled loose from the register underneath the floor.
  5. Pull out or examine the filter as part of your air handler inspection. Many times the filter is the wrong size or clogged beyond belief. A clogged filter can cause $10 a month in electricity cost and shorten the life of the unit, not to mention poor air quality.
  6. New construction: Make sure you try to look deep inside the return air cavity in the wall to look for unhealthy items left behind by sub contractors.
  7. Radiators for old boilers can clog or not heat fully. Sometimes they can be blown clean by a boiler technician and sometimes they cannot. One radiator could cost $1000 or more easily ($80 a rung so I've heard) so be sure and write up any that do not get hot on both ends as needing servicing or further inspection by a Boiler technician.
  8. Read the auto-comments in the heat section.

II-F81BD7BC-5B0A-4E6A-A79B-2D1784031032.title: GARAGE DOOR OPERATORS (Report whether or not doors will reverse when met with resistance)
II-F81BD7BC-5B0A-4E6A-A79B-2D1784031032.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is the auto-opener using a light fixture adapter or an extension cord that's not approved?

2. Look for a missing cover, burnt cover, missing bulb etc.

3. Look for the electrical plug and make sure it has a proper outlet in reach.

4. Some doors do not reverse when met with resistance and could kill. Always be concerned about that.

5. The reason why the door needs to reverse when met with resistance, even with sensors in place, is because if a truck bed or bumper was extended into the door path and is higher than the sensors, major damage would occur.

6. Doors that need adjustment in order to reverse may not be able to be adjusted. Sometimes the adjustment screws/knobs will not adjust it properly.

7. Check for height to accommodate most vehicles or let them know a large car may not fit.

II-F964B3A1-3F0B-4383-B0F6-5FCF638C2E19.title: BRANCH CIRCUIT CONDUCTORS,  OVERCURRENT DEVICES AND COMPATIBILITY OF THEIR AMPERAGE AND VOLTAGE
II-F964B3A1-3F0B-4383-B0F6-5FCF638C2E19.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is there doubled wiring at circuits? 14 Gauge = 15 amp, 12 Gauge = 20 amp, 10 gauge = 30 amp?

2. You must use solid copper tubing wire not strand wire on 30 amp circuits or less.

3. Note any fuses in panel that are Edison based (interchangeable).

4. Are branch circuits labeled, identifying the locations?

5. Note any circuits that were turned off and not tested during inspection.

6. Federal Pacific electric panels are unsafe. An excellent source of info iswww.inspect-ny.com

More Info:

  1. Are you new to Electrical? If so, I recommend studying the basics of wiring and circuit breakers.
  2. 14 Gauge=15 amp breakers and 12 gauge=20 amp breakers and so on.
  3. Go to Lowe's or building Depot or your building supply store and hang out in the electrical wiring isle. Touch grab and feel.
  4. You could call up a few different electrical contractors (small outfits) and introduce yourself and your company and ask him if he would be interested in coaching you from time to time in exchange for referrals or a fee. Until you learn when to recommend an electrical contractor, you can explain to the buyer that this wiring method at the panel looks unfamiliar and you want to hold off on your condition call until you speak to an electrical contractor. Then call the electrical contractor and ask him. If possible, email him a picture of it if there is enough time allowed. This is how you learn. Pass all panels that appear to be wired properly based on what is proper, and recommend an electrical contractor on everything else.

II-F9A2B0DE-03AF-48D4-B76A-EC7332F6869B.title: COOLING EQUIPMENT
II-F9A2B0DE-03AF-48D4-B76A-EC7332F6869B.helpHtml: Central Air should not be ran if outside temperature is at 65 degrees or less. You could damage the unit. Be sure and note if you did not inspect it. Turn on A/C and wait about 15 minutes or so. Grab and hold the suction line just before it enters air handler inside and feel for ice cold. (This will tell you if the compressor outside is making cold air). No cold feeling could mean  a number of things that will involve servicing the unit (low on refrigerant, leak, compressor problem etc.) Only trouble shooting by a qualified heat contractor can determine exactly. Recommend service. If the suction line is iced over where it enters Air Handler, the coils inside air handler may need cleaning. To check for ambient air, you would need the A/C to run longer than 15 minutes or so. Insert a thermometer in the supply plenum, and then insert another thermometer into the return-air plenum. The Return air should be within 20-25 degrees of the thermometer in the supply plenum. The amount of time the A/C would need to run before checking ambient air will vary, depending upon how hot it is inside when you first ran the A/C. This may require an hour or so to give the A/C a chance to work at it's potential.

II-F9F782F3-99B4-481C-9B31-41756A6F5ABB.title: SERVICE ENTRANCE CONDUCTORS
II-F9F782F3-99B4-481C-9B31-41756A6F5ABB.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Are the electric service conductors too low to the ground or deck or too close to a window?

2. Is the meterbase secure on the wall?

3. Is a drip loop present at weather head?

4. Is the wall anchor in place?

More Info:

The home inspector shall describe: Service amperage and voltage; Service entry conductor materials; Service type as being overhead or underground; and Location of main and distribution panels. The home inspector shall report any observed aluminum branch circuit wiring. The home inspector shall report on presence or absence of smoke detectors, and operate their test function, if accessible, except when detectors are part of a central system.

The home inspector is not required to: Insert any tool, probe, or testing device inside the panels; Test or operate any overcurrent device except ground fault circuit interrupters; Dismantle any electrical device or control other than to remove the covers of the main and auxiliary distribution panels; or Observe: Low voltage systems; Security system devices, heat detectors, or carbon monoxide detectors; Telephone, security, cable TV, intercoms, or other ancillary wiring that is not a part of the primary electrical distribution system; or Built-in vacuum equipment.

II-FB461357-AA78-4E26-9B53-5B24EA004BA0.title: VENTILATION FANS AND THERMOSTATIC CONTROLS (ATTIC)
II-FB461357-AA78-4E26-9B53-5B24EA004BA0.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

More Info:

  1. Thermostatically controlled fans in the attic may not turn on if the attic is colder than the lowest setting.
  2. Spin the blade by hand to see if it is seized or turns freely.
  3. Seized fans mean repair or replacement.
  4. Also, humming or hot fans when not on, is a sign of a problem.
  5. Make sure you don't turn on a whole house fan when the attic hole is uncovered or you will be fiberglass-blasted (been there, done that).
  6. Make sure the buyer doesn't turn on the switch while you're up in attic (been there too).
  7. Some people will cover the whole house fan blade with blankets or plastic during winter to prevent heat loss. If you turn on the switch before checking, you could damage the unit.

II-FC041887-CDC5-46EF-A9FA-4D806D16BFCD.title: ROOF COVERINGS
II-FC041887-CDC5-46EF-A9FA-4D806D16BFCD.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Are there any noticeable sways or sags in the roof?

2. Do you estimate the life remaining on the roof covering to be 4 years or less?

3. Are there any repair signs on the roof?

4. Are there any sides or areas of the roof that were not inspected due to no access?

More Info:

  1. I don't get up on all roofs, but many if not most of the roofs I see are accessible. These are walkable roofs and not too steep.
  2. Hair-line cracks that sometimes occur on shingles cannot be seen unless you go up on the roof. Caulking or repair signs can be missed as well. If you're on the roof, look for boot flange for vent pipes to see if they fit the pipe to keep out rain.
  3. I don't walk on tile roofs or wood shakes for fear of damaging them or falling.
  4. Never step out on a metal awning.

Reference Materials:

The building inspector shall observe: Roof covering; Roof drainage systems; Flashings; Skylights, chimneys, and roof penetrations; and signs of' leaks or abnormal condensation on building components. The building inspector shall: Describe the type of roof covering materials; and Report the methods used to observe the roofing.

The building inspector is not required to: Walk on the roofing; or Observe attached accessories including but not limited to solar systems, antennae, and lightning arrestors.

II-FD30077B-5F42-48EC-B555-DF7F5C41B95C.title: INTERIOR WATER SUPPLY AND DISTRIBUTION SYSTEMS AND FIXTURES
II-FD30077B-5F42-48EC-B555-DF7F5C41B95C.helpHtml: The home inspector shall observe: Interior water supply and distribution system, including: piping materials, supports, and insulation; fixtures and faucets; functional flow; leaks; and cross connections; Interior drain, waste, and vent system, including: traps; drain, waste, and vent piping; piping supports and pipe insulation; leaks; and functional drainage; Hot water systems including: water heating equipment; normal operating controls; automatic safety controls; and chimneys, flues, and vents; Fuel storage and distribution systems including: interior fuel storage equipment, supply piping, venting, and supports; leaks; and Sump pumps.The home inspector shall describe: Water supply and distribution piping materials; Drain, waste, and vent piping materials; Water heating equipment; and Location of main water supply shutoff device. The home inspector shall operate all plumbing fixtures, including their faucets and all exterior faucets attached to the house, except where the flow end of the faucet is connected to an appliance.The home inspector is not required to: State the effectiveness of anti-siphon devices; Determine whether water supply and waste disposal systems are public or private; Operate automatic safety controls; Operate any valve except water closet flush valves, fixture faucets, and hose faucets; Observe: Water conditioning systems; Fire and lawn sprinkler systems; On-site water supply quantity and quality; On-site waste disposal systems; Foundation irrigation systems; Spas, except as to functional flow and functional drainage; Swimming pools; Solar water heating equipment; or Observe the system for proper sizing, design, or use of proper materials.

II-FD419D15-B768-4BBB-AE95-272797184CF9.title: PRESENCE OF INSTALLED HVAC SOURCE IN EACH ROOM
II-FD419D15-B768-4BBB-AE95-272797184CF9.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

More Info:

  1. Don't miss the absence of a vent in a room or you could be sued and be liable for the cost to put one in.
  2. One must also consider: Why isn't one there? It could be the size of the heat/AC unit which would require a bigger unit or perhaps there is no physical way to install one. Extreme remodeling may be involved.
  3. Also, stay alert for the type of heating system in the house with an AC condenser. If it's boiler heat and there is an AC unit outside, and the house is 2 story, it is likely that the AC serves the upstairs only. Therefore it is necessary to point this out in your report.

II-FDE0C911-3ED6-4F1B-8A06-8A3F621AFAB1.title: FLOORS
II-FDE0C911-3ED6-4F1B-8A06-8A3F621AFAB1.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Note any settlement cracks in garage floor.

2. Is vinyl floor curling in the tub area?

3. Does the tile floor need grout and sealant?

4. Is there silicone caulk along the tub?

5. Inspect the floor under window locations?

More Info:

  1. Look at an old building with an old eye.
  2. Always note water stains.
  3. On newer homes, note nail pops, exposed or loose sheetrock tape and repair signs.
  4. Workmanship is important in all homes but especially new ones.
  5. Look for signs of only one coat of paint, poor sanding, nail indentations etc.
  6. Look at the perimeter of floor for water stains or deterioration.
  7. Bounce around a little on the floor (without lifting your feet).
  8. Note any areas damaged on floor covering, including stains, exposed seams, small tears or blemishes etc.

II-FE0D3898-B611-4BFC-A55D-9F97C40EF8F3.title: HEATING EQUIPMENT
II-FE0D3898-B611-4BFC-A55D-9F97C40EF8F3.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Is the heat pump / condenser level?

2. Are the foam sleeves on the suction line intact?

3. Are bushes or a fence obstructing air flow?

4. Hydronic systems should have a water heater that is designed for heating the home and not use converted water heaters. Converted water heaters may not have a high enough BTU rating.

5. Are there any electric outlets located on the wall above the electric baseboard which could be a possible fire hazard?

More Info:

  1. Heating Equipment over 15 years old and still operating should still be noted as old, and recommend servicing them annually to monitor for safe operation.
  2. (Oil furnaces) Check around the sight hole for smoke stains around the collar that may be leaking fumes.
  3. Examine the vent pipe and where it enters chimney for integrity and proper seal.
  4. Check for back drafting by using a lighter or match around joints in the vent pipe, or at an existing test hole (if any).
  5. An erratic movement of the damper lid on the vent pipe and/or soot build-up should be noted.
  6. The furnace should run for at least 15 minutes.
  7. It's a good technique to observe the firing, or ignition, of the furnace. To do this, use the cut-off switch at the furnace before you set the thermostat to turn the furnace on. If it's not running normally, recommend a licensed heat contractor for service and repair as needed.
  8. Learn how to perform a smoke bomb test. Use a Gas Tracer.
  9. ( GAS FURNACES ) Use a gas tracer around the unit. Examine burners and raceway for charred bits and recommend service if bits are excessive or flame is not even.
  10. If flame dances sharply or rolls under the burner recommend service.
  11. Heat exchangers or the steel liner is more likely to crack near the pilot light.
  12. ( BOILERS ) should be tested for 30 to 45 minutes to allow all radiators to heat fully. Some radiators that are old may take longer to heat but you have to decide while your there if they heat from one end to the other. This time is needed to allow pressure to build and check for leaks. Radiators are extremely expensive and you don't want to miss even one. If over 15 years old and operating well it should be noted as old and recommend servicing annually to monitor for safe operation.
  13. Check around the sight hole for smoke stains around the collar that may be leaking fumes. Examine the vent pipe and where it enters the chimney for integrity and proper seal.
  14. Check for back drafting by using a lighter or match around joints in the vent pipe, or at an existing test hole (if any).
  15. Steam boilers have a sight glass to check water level.
  16. Circulating boilers do not have a sight glass.
  17. Boilers should be flushed regularly as part of a normal maintenance schedule.
  18. ( HEAT PUMPS ) should not be ran in AC mode if temp outside is @ 65 degrees or less. You could damage the unit.
  19. Be sure and note if you did not inspect it. Just because you have heat coming out of the registers doesn't mean your compressor outside is working.
  20. The fan outside should be moving. Just because the fan outside is moving doesn't mean you have heat.
  21. Grab the suction line before it enters air handler inside and feel for heat.
  22. In summer, hand check the suction line for ice cold. No cold feeling means recommending service.
  23. The coils inside the air handler may need cleaning or the liquid line may need refrigerant.
  24. Only trouble shooting by a qualified heat contractor can determine exactly.
  25. The ambient air test differential on a heat pump should be between 14 and 22 degrees. Use a thermometer at the main plenum and use one at the return air at the air handler. The difference in these (in AC mode) should be 14 to 22 degrees.
  26. ( ELECTRIC BASE ) should be turned on and checked for proper operation, securely fastened to wall or floor.
  27. There should never be an outlet on the wall directly above electric base.
  28. Remove the front cover on the baseboard and inspect the wire that runs the length of the base located inside a tube. This wire can become brittle or weak over time, and cause abnormal heating up of unit and can cause a fire.

Reference Materials:

The home inspector shall observe permanently installed heating systems including: Heating equipment; Normal operating controls; Automatic safety controls; Chimneys, flues, and vents, where readily visible; Solid fuel heating devices; Heat distribution systems including fans, pumps, ducts and piping, with supports, insulation, air filters, registers, radiators, fan coil units, convectors; and the presence of an installed heat source in each room. The home inspector shall describe: Energy source; and Heating equipment and distribution type. The home inspector shall operate the systems using normal operating controls. The home inspector shall open readily openable access panels provided by the manufacturer or installer for routine homeowner maintenance.

The home inspector is not required to: Operate heating systems when weather conditions or other circumstances may cause equipment damage; Operate automatic safety controls; Ignite or extinguish solid fuel fires; or Observe: The interior of flues; Fireplace insert flue connections; Humidifiers; Electronic air filters; or The uniformity or adequacy of heat supply to the various rooms.

II-FE226904-CFDD-468F-BCAB-62CECFA524E3.title: DISTRIBUTION SYSTEMS (including fans, pumps, ducts and piping, with supports, insulation, air filters, registers, radiators, fan coil units and convectors)
II-FE226904-CFDD-468F-BCAB-62CECFA524E3.helpHtml:
Quick Check:

1. Inspect filter condition and look for a good seal around the filter door or compartment?

2. Is there damaged or loose ductwork, duct tape?

3. Does the furnace or airhandler shut off when the blower door is removed (safety switch)?

More Info:

  1. Make sure you note if a room does not have a register or vent.
  2. Also inspect all ductwork accessible. Note if the ductwork is not insulated if there is AC.
  3. Many times the tape is failing and the ductpipe has pulled loose from the register underneath the floor.
  4. Pull out or examine the filter as part of your air handler inspection. Many times the filter is the wrong size or clogged beyond belief.
  5. A clogged filter can cause $10 a month in electricity costs and shorten the life of the unit not to mention the poor air quality.
  6. New construction: Make sure you try to look deep inside the return air cavity in the wall to look for unhealthy items left behind by sub contractors.
  7. Radiators for old boilers can clog or not heat fully. Sometimes they can be blown clean by a boiler technician and sometimes they cannot. One radiator could cost $1000 or more easily ($80 a rung so I've heard) so be sure and write up any that do not get hot on both ends as needing servicing or further inspection by a Boiler technician.
  8. Read the auto-comments in the heat section.
